# HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

Jianghan Zhu    Cong Zhang    Ni Zhang    Yifan Yang    Yew Soon Ong   
Zhiguang Cao ^(†)^(†)thanks: Jianghan Zhu, Ni Zhang, and Zhiguang Cao
are with the School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore
Management University, Singapore. (E-mail:
[zhuj0044@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:zhuj0044@ntu.edu.sg))^(†)^(†)thanks: Yifan
Yang, and Yew Soon Ong are with the College of Computing and Data
Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.^(†)^(†)thanks:
Cong Zhang used to be affiliated with Nanyang Technological University,
Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab, and TikTok Singapore. Now he is an independent
researcher.

###### Abstract

Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language
models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation
operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet
most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that
discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs
and operator interactions change where and how the search should
proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a
self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness
state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that
determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve,
which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of
search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these
updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward
promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory
filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across
harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated
optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two
structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong
performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD
baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO
extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators
to improving the search process that discovers them.

###### Index Terms: 

Evolutionary computing and genetic algorithms, heuristics design,
heuristic methods, language models, multi-objective combinatorial
optimization, optimization.

## I Introduction

Multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) arises in many
discrete decision problems with competing objectives, including routing,
scheduling, and resource allocation \[[1](#bib.bib55), [2](#bib.bib57),
[3](#bib.bib52), [4](#bib.bib56)\]. A spectrum of methods has been
developed for these problems, including exact
approaches \[[5](#bib.bib49)\], Pareto local search and related
metaheuristics \[[6](#bib.bib58)\], and population-based evolutionary
algorithms such as NSGA-II and MOEA/D \[[7](#bib.bib15),
[8](#bib.bib16)\]. Despite their different search mechanisms,
performance often relies on problem-specific representations, and
variation operators, making the solving of a new MOCO problem closely
tied to the design of an effective search procedure.

Learning-based combinatorial optimization has sought to reduce this
manual effort by learning solution policies directly from
data \[[9](#bib.bib23), [10](#bib.bib24), [11](#bib.bib5)\] while
automatic algorithm design (AAD), particularly automatic heuristic
design (AHD), instead automates the generation and improvement of
algorithmic components \[[12](#bib.bib8)\]. Recent LLM-based methods
further enable evolutionary search over algorithms and
heuristics \[[13](#bib.bib10), [14](#bib.bib11), [15](#bib.bib12)\].
Within MOCO, a particularly relevant direction is the automatic design
of problem-specific search and variation operators, which we refer to as
automatic operator design (AOD). LLMs have been used to generate
evolutionary operators with different trade-offs \[[16](#bib.bib54),
[17](#bib.bib32)\], while newer frameworks further emphasize population
diversity and operator interactions \[[18](#bib.bib34),
[19](#bib.bib36)\]. These developments mark a shift from generating
isolated heuristics toward designing structured optimization components.

LLM-based AOD relies on an outer control process that determines how
design context is formed, when candidates are evaluated, how search
state is recorded, and when search terminates. We call this control
process the _AOD harness_, specializing the broader notion of an LLM
harness as executable infrastructure governing model context,
environment interactions, and control flow \[[20](#bib.bib46),
[21](#bib.bib41)\] to the search over operator candidates. Most
evolutionary AOD methods use a largely fixed harness, with the main
operator search steps governed by predefined procedures. For example,
AlphaEvolve retains a fixed search framework in which the model context
is assembled through predefined selection rules \[[22](#bib.bib61)\].
Greater LLM autonomy can also be introduced within a fixed search loop,
whereas recent methods search over independently generated
abstraction-level heuristic-optimizers that serve as fixed search
controllers for the inner AHD process \[[23](#bib.bib14)\].
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
summarizes these regimes along two dimensions, namely _agent autonomy in
search control_ and _AOD harness adaptivity_.

This distinction matters for MOCO-oriented AOD, where the search state
changes continuously as new trade-offs, candidate structures, and
component interactions emerge. The effectiveness of a search decision
can vary over time, and a strategy that works well at one stage may
become less suitable as the explored regions and candidate population
change.

![Refer to caption](2610.40023v1/hemo_compare2.png)

Fig. 1: Paradigms of LLM-based AOD characterized by agent autonomy and
harness adaptivity. Fixed evolutionary AOD (upper left) uses agents as
role-specific tools within a predefined evolutionary loop, whereas
independent AOD harness search (upper right) evaluates separately
sampled but internally fixed harnesses. Agent-autonomic AOD (lower left)
allows the agent to control candidate generation and feedback inspection
within a fixed outer AOD loop, while stateful AOD harness
self-evolution, adopted by HEMO in the lower-right quadrant, evolves the
stateful harness itself through persistent module-level transitions,
allowing search control and the use of accumulated experience to
co-adapt over time under outer-agent guidance.

A fixed AOD harness cannot revise its predefined control logic, while
independently generated high-level procedures lack a persistent
control-state trajectory. This motivates a stateful AOD harness that
evolves its search behavior as optimization experience accumulates. Such
self-evolution also requires access to relevant long-term experience. An
AOD run may produce hundreds or thousands of evaluated candidates with
their performance, lineage, and search context, yet storing this history
alone does not ensure useful evidence remains accessible. Recent harness
research likewise emphasizes detailed execution records and selective
retrieval in long-running searches \[[20](#bib.bib46),
[24](#bib.bib45)\]. For MOCO, relevant evidence can span Pareto regions,
complementary candidates, and earlier search stages, making persistent,
selectively retrieved experience a stable basis for adapting harness
decisions.

Motivated by these observations, we introduce HEMO, a stateful AOD
harness for LLM-based operator design in multi-objective combinatorial
optimization. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and
progressively adapts its search control through localized state
transitions. Successive harness states are assessed by their downstream
impact on multi-objective operator design, while optimization experience
from evaluated candidates is continuously retained in a _memory
filesystem_ and selectively reused by subsequent states. This
formulation allows the AOD harness to adapt across different search
stages while the memory filesystem evolves with the trajectory and
preserves a consistent archive of optimization experience, thereby
improving how an LLM-driven operator design process searches, learns
from feedback, and reuses experience over time.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We introduce a _stateful harness self-evolution_ perspective for LLM
  driven AOD. The AOD harness maintains a persistent state and evolves
  through local updates along a single harness design trajectory,
  extending beyond fixed outer procedures, agent-directed search within
  fixed harnesses, and independently evaluated high-level search
  procedures.
- •
  We develop HEMO, a framework designed specifically for MOCO using
  downstream multi-objective AOD performance to guide harness state
  adaptation while preserving long-term experience in a memory
  filesystem. Later search decisions can thus draw on evidence from
  previous harness states without compressing the full history into a
  limited recent context.
- •
  Extensive experiments on eight MOCO tasks spanning routing, traveling
  salesman, knapsack, and scheduling, using two representative
  evolutionary backbones, demonstrate the effectiveness of HEMO across
  diverse settings against conventional evolutionary, neural, and
  LLM-based AOD baselines in both within-task evaluation and cross-task
  transfer.

## II Related Work

### II-A Automated Algorithm Design

Automated algorithm design (AAD) aims to reduce the expert effort
required to construct effective algorithms by automating design
processes such as algorithm selection, configuration, component design,
and code execution and validation \[[25](#bib.bib7), [26](#bib.bib9),
[27](#bib.bib67)\]. Automated heuristic design (AHD) forms an important
research branch of this broader field, with methods ranging from
hyper-heuristics \[[12](#bib.bib8)\] and genetic
programming \[[26](#bib.bib9)\] to the automatic generation and
composition of search operators \[[28](#bib.bib66)\]. Although these
approaches automate different parts of algorithm development, the
underlying heuristic spaces and composition rules are commonly specified
by human experts.

LLM reasoning and code generation have substantially expanded the scope
of automated design. FunSearch evolves executable programs through
island-based selection and generation \[[13](#bib.bib10)\], while EoH,
ReEvo, and MCTS-AHD combine LLM generation with evolutionary,
reflective, or tree-based search to improve one single-objective
optimization heuristic component \[[14](#bib.bib11), [15](#bib.bib12),
[29](#bib.bib13)\]. SimpleEvol further organizes LLM-driven heuristic
generation within a lightweight agent loop designed to minimize
human-specified priors \[[30](#bib.bib6)\]. Beyond individual
combinatorial heuristics, LLaMEA and LLaMEA-BO evolve complete
algorithms for continuous black-box and Bayesian optimization,
respectively \[[31](#bib.bib59), [32](#bib.bib60)\]. Outside
optimization, AlphaEvolve demonstrates evolutionary code search over
broader scientific and computational algorithms \[[22](#bib.bib61)\].
More recent work has begun to move the design target beyond solely
heuristics. MoH searches over heuristic optimizers that generate
task-specific heuristics \[[23](#bib.bib14)\], while related work
explores higher-level algorithm structures and control
policies \[[33](#bib.bib62)\]. These developments indicate a broader
shift from designing isolated heuristics toward changing increasingly
large portions of the algorithm design process itself. Yet the execution
structure governing LLM access to accumulated experience, forms design
context, invokes evaluation, and maintains search state is still
typically specified by human designers. Designing a framework that
enables the stateful self-evolution of this surrounding control
structure is therefore the focus of our work.

### II-B Multi-Objective Optimization

Most of recent research can be divided into two pathways. The first
improves multi-objective solvers through manually designed evolutionary
mechanisms or learned solution policies and search components. Classical
multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) include dominance-based
methods such as NSGA-II \[[7](#bib.bib15)\], decomposition-based methods
like MOEA/D \[[8](#bib.bib16)\], and archive- or local-search-based
approaches such as Pareto Local Search (PLS) \[[34](#bib.bib17)\],
two-phase Pareto Local Search (2PPLS) \[[3](#bib.bib52)\], and Simple
Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization (SEMO) \[[35](#bib.bib18)\].
Their effectiveness depends strongly on carefully designed mechanisms
for selection, population management, neighborhood exploration, and
diversity preservation, motivating numerous modified and hybrid
variants \[[36](#bib.bib19), [37](#bib.bib65)\]. Neural approaches
instead learn solution policies or search components from data. PMOCO
employs a single preference-conditioned model to generate solutions
under different objective preferences \[[9](#bib.bib23)\]. NHDE
explicitly promotes Pareto-set diversity \[[10](#bib.bib24)\], while
EMNH improves learning efficiency through
meta-learning \[[38](#bib.bib28)\].Neuro-PLS embeds learned components
into Pareto local search \[[39](#bib.bib29)\], while other work improves
preference conditioning and cross-size generalization through learned
weight representations \[[40](#bib.bib30)\]. Although neural methods
reduce repeated handcrafting and enable fast GPU-based inference, they
generally require model training and retain a largely predefined
optimization backbone.

The second pathway uses LLMs to design problem-specific heuristics and
variation operators within prescribed multi-objective solvers, a setting
we refer to as automatic operator design (AOD). Here, an operator is an
algorithmic component that constructs, modifies, selects, or otherwise
guides candidate solutions, including heuristics studied in AHD when
they serve such a role. Huang et al. \[[16](#bib.bib54)\] use LLMs to
iteratively refine evolutionary operators. MEoH treats heuristic design
as a multi-objective optimization problem and searches for non-dominated
heuristics \[[17](#bib.bib32)\], while REMoH integrates LLM-generated
operators into NSGA-II with clustering-based reflection to promote
diversity \[[41](#bib.bib33)\]. MPaGE combines LLM-based heuristic
generation with Pareto-front-grid-guided population management under
SEMO \[[18](#bib.bib34)\]. E2OC further models dependencies among
multiple search operators and uses Monte Carlo tree search to explore
their design combinations \[[19](#bib.bib36)\]. These methods extend
LLM-based AAD toward increasingly complex multi-objective solver
components. However, they primarily evolve operators _within_ a
prescribed search process, leaving its higher-level harness unchanged.

### II-C Harness Engineering and Evolution

The performance of an LLM-based system depends not only on its backbone
model, but also on the surrounding execution machinery that determines
what information the model receives, which tools it can invoke, how
intermediate state is recorded and updated, and how multi-step execution
is guided by feedback. Mechanisms now associated with this layer were
initially studied separately, including retrieval-augmented
generation \[[42](#bib.bib37)\], interleaved reasoning and
acting \[[43](#bib.bib38)\], and explicit
self-reflection \[[44](#bib.bib39)\]. Recent work increasingly
integrates these mechanisms into a broader _agent harness_.
Natural-Language Agent Harnesses separate control, contracts, and
persistent state from the underlying runtime \[[45](#bib.bib40)\], while
recent surveys characterize harness engineering as spanning execution
environments, tool interfaces, context and memory management, lifecycle
and orchestration, execution monitoring, and output
validation \[[21](#bib.bib41)\]. A closely related line of work also
automates broader portions of agent and optimization
systems \[[46](#bib.bib3), [47](#bib.bib2)\]. ADAS searches over
code-defined agent systems \[[48](#bib.bib42)\], AFlow formulates
agentic workflow generation as search over executable workflow
graphs \[[49](#bib.bib43)\], and the Darwin Gödel Machine allows coding
agents to iteratively modify their own
implementations \[[50](#bib.bib44)\]. In optimization, AutoEP uses an
external LLM-based controller to adapt the hyperparameters of a
structurally fixed metaheuristic \[[51](#bib.bib51)\], while OKAEM
adapts learned evolutionary operators using prior and online
optimization knowledge \[[52](#bib.bib4)\]. CORAL employs autonomous
single- and multi-agent evolution to determine what experience to
retrieve, when to evaluate candidates, and what knowledge to
preserve \[[24](#bib.bib45)\]. Although these approaches automate
context construction, workflows, and search control, they do not
generally treat the complete task-specific execution harness as the
direct search object.

More recent studies explicitly optimize the harness surrounding an LLM.
Meta-Harness performs outer-loop search over harness code, allowing an
agentic proposer to inspect previous source code, evaluation scores, and
execution traces through a filesystem before constructing new harness
candidates \[[20](#bib.bib46)\]. Self-Harness similarly identifies
recurring weaknesses from execution traces, proposes targeted
modifications, and validates the resulting harness \[[53](#bib.bib47)\].
Existing harness evolution studies primarily target general agent
execution in coding, reasoning, and interactive tasks. HEMO instead
studies harness evolution for LLM-based automatic operator design in
MOCO. It maintains a persistent AOD harness whose decision modules adapt
through localized state transitions while the execution-critical
scaffold remains fixed, connecting harness adaptation directly to
downstream multi-objective optimization performance and long-term
operator design experience.

## III Preliminaries

### III-A Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

Problem Formulation and Pareto Optimality. A multi-objective
combinatorial optimization problem (MOCOP) seeks to optimize multiple,
potentially conflicting objectives over a discrete feasible
space \[[54](#bib.bib48)\]. Let $`\mathcal{X}`$ be the feasible solution
set and $`M`$ the number of objectives. Without loss of generality, we
consider the minimization form

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\left(f_{1}(\mathbf{x}),f_{2}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,f_{M}(\mathbf{x})\right).
``` |  | (1) |

For two feasible solutions $`\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{X}`$,
$`\mathbf{x}`$ is said to *Pareto-dominate* $`\mathbf{y}`$, denoted by
$`\mathbf{x}\prec\mathbf{y}`$, if

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{m}(\mathbf{x})\leq f_{m}(\mathbf{y}),\quad\forall m\in\{1,\ldots,M\},
``` |  | (2) |

and the inequality is strict for at least one objective. A feasible
solution $`\mathbf{x}^{*}`$ is *Pareto optimal* if there exists no other
feasible solution that dominates it. The collection of all
Pareto-optimal solutions constitutes the *Pareto set* (PS), and its
image in the objective space constitutes the *Pareto front* (PF).

For many MOCOPs, computing the complete Pareto set is computationally
prohibitive, and practical solvers therefore seek a finite approximation
of the PF under limited computational budgets \[[5](#bib.bib49),
[55](#bib.bib50)\]. A useful approximation should simultaneously
approach the true PF and maintain sufficient coverage across different
trade-offs among objectives \[[55](#bib.bib50)\].

Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms. Multi-objective evolutionary
algorithms (MOEAs) construct such approximations by evolving a
population or archive of candidate solutions. Early Pareto-based
evolutionary approaches established selection at the population level
based on dominance and diversity, with later methods developing
alternative mechanisms to balance convergence and diversity. The MOEA
behavior thus depends on both problem-specific variation operators and
higher-level mechanisms to select, retain, and propagate solutions
across iterations. We use two structurally distinct backbones, namely
SEMO \[[35](#bib.bib18)\], with incremental archive updates, and
NSGA-II \[[7](#bib.bib15)\], which uses generational population
evolution with non-dominated sorting and diversity preservation.

### III-B AOD Harnesses

Agent Harnesses. An LLM-based system includes an execution layer that
governs the context presented to the model, interactions with tools and
evaluators, persistent state, and control across multiple model calls.
We refer to this execution layer as an *agent harness*. In automatic
operator design, the harness governs the outer process through which an
LLM searches over operator candidates. It determines how prior search
experience is exposed, how design context is assembled, how candidate
generation and evaluation are coordinated, and how search state is
maintained across iterations. We use the term *AOD harness* for this
task-specific execution structure. The methodology in
Section [IV](#S4 "IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
focuses on how such a harness can maintain a persistent state and adapt
its search-control behavior over time.

## IV Methodology

HEMO is an AOD harness with self-evolving decision modules for
multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Its state evolves
through local module updates, while a memory filesystem retains
experience across states. These updates adapt experience retrieval,
target and parent selection, and candidate evolution, with new
optimization experience continuously recorded in memory.

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
summarizes the overall workflow. HEMO separates a fixed execution
scaffold from the set of decision modules, with harness state
transitions guided by the module-specific reward computed from
downstream task performance. Three LLM agents play distinct roles in
this process. The Proposer Agent specifies an updated version of one
selected module in a JSON blueprint using the current harness state,
task information, and recent harness traces. The Realizer Agent converts
this blueprint into executable Python code grounded in the current
harness implementation. The resulting child harness is then
operationalized by the Executor Agent within a bounded harness
evaluation episode, interacting with the memory filesystem and the task
evaluator, and producing evaluated candidates and search records. Memory
persists across episodes, accumulating experience along the outer
trajectory.

![Refer to caption](2610.40023v1/hemo_workflow2.png)

Fig. 2: Overview of HEMO. Along the outer state transition trajectory, a
selected decision module is revised and incorporated into the parent
harness to form the child harness for the next evaluation episode, while
optimization experience is retained in the memory filesystem.

### IV-A Stateful Harness Self-Evolution

Harness initialization. HEMO begins from a manually specified seed
harness that defines the basic execution interface and a simple
reference implementation for each evolvable module. To avoid committing
the search to a single manually designed starting point, a small set of
alternative harness blueprints, each specifying all evolvable modules,
is generated and realized to form an initial harness pool. These states
are evaluated to construct an initial Pareto archive over harness
states, from which the initial current state $`H_{0}`$ is selected for
subsequent harness self-evolution.

Harness state transitions. We represent the current harness state as
$`H_{t}=(C_{t},B_{t})`$, where $`C_{t}`$ denotes the full harness code
and $`B_{t}`$ denotes its corresponding blueprint that records the
current specifications of all evolvable modules. The memory filesystem
at step $`t`$ is denoted by $`M_{t}`$ and serves as an external
mechanism for retaining optimization experience across harness states.
At each outer step after initialization, one evolvable module
$`m_{t}\in\mathcal{M}`$ is selected for modification, where
$`\mathcal{M}=\{m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(K)}\}`$ denotes the set of evolvable
modules. The Proposer Agent generates a module blueprint
$`b_{t}=\mathcal{P}(H_{t},m_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t})`$, where
$`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$ contains the task description and recent harness
evaluations. The Realizer Agent converts this blueprint into an
executable replacement $`\phi_{t}`$, yielding

|     |                                                |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H^{\prime}_{t}=H_{t}[m_{t}\leftarrow\phi_{t}].
       ```                                             |     | (3) |

After evaluating $`H^{\prime}_{t}`$, it becomes the next current harness
state if its parent $`H_{t}`$ does not Pareto-dominate it. The outer
Pareto archive is updated with the evaluated child according to Pareto
dominance. The resulting state transition is

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (H_{t},M_{t})\rightarrow(H_{t+1},M_{t+1}),
       ```                                         |     |

where an accepted harness modification updates the harness state and
newly generated experience updates the memory filesystem. This localized
transition preserves accumulated harness behavior, makes consecutive
states directly comparable, and localizes credit to the modified module.

Downstream harness evaluation. Let $`\mathcal{P}(H^{\prime}_{t})`$
denote the final Pareto archive of operator candidates produced during
the evaluation episode of $`H^{\prime}_{t}`$. We use the hypervolume
(HV) indicator together with runtime to summarize harness performance.
The summarization score is computed by averaging these quantities over
the final candidate Pareto archive:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{s}(H^{\prime}_{t})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}(H^{\prime}_{t})|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{P}(H^{\prime}_{t})}\left(-\mathrm{HV}(a),\mathrm{Runtime}(a)\right).
``` |  | (4) |

Both dimensions follow a lower-is-better convention. To obtain
scale-insensitive credit for the selected module, HEMO computes the
normalized parent-to-child improvement along each evaluation dimension:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{t,d}=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{s_{d}(H_{t})-s_{d}(H^{\prime}_{t})}{\max\!\left(|s_{d}(H_{t})|,|s_{d}(H^{\prime}_{t})|\right)},-1,1\right).
``` |  | (5) |

The reward at module level is then aggregated as

|     |                                         |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{t}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}r_{t,d}.
       ```                                      |     | (6) |

The scalar reward $`r_{t}`$ is used only for adaptive module credit
assignment, while the original multi-dimensional harness evaluation is
retained for Pareto-based comparison and archival throughout the outer
search process.

Adaptive Scheduler via Discounted UCB. The Adaptive Scheduler determines
which evolvable module is updated at each outer step. The utility of a
module changes as the other modules in the harness are modified, making
module selection inherently non-stationary \[[56](#bib.bib1)\]. We
therefore instantiate the scheduler with discounted
UCB \[[57](#bib.bib63)\], which favors recent module outcomes while
retaining an exploration bonus for less frequently selected modules. For
each module $`m`$, HEMO maintains a discounted selection count
$`n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}`$ and discounted reward sum $`R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}`$.
At each outer step, both statistics are multiplied by a discount factor
$`\gamma\in(0,1)`$, after which the selected module receives one
additional visit and its current reward. Its discounted mean reward is
$`\bar{r}^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}=R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}/n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}.`$ The
next module is selected according to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{UCB}_{t}(m)=\bar{r}^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}+c\sqrt{\frac{\log\!\left(1+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}}n^{(\gamma)}_{j,t}\right)}{n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}}},
``` |  | (7) |

where $`c`$ controls exploration strength. Each module is selected
exactly once before applying
Eq. ([7](#S4.E7 "In IV-A Stateful Harness Self-Evolution ‣ IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")).
Discounting is used because the reward of updating a module depends on
the current harness state. A module that was unproductive earlier may
become useful again after other modules have changed. Older observations
are therefore gradually downweighted instead of remaining equally
influential throughout the evolution trajectory.
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Why Discounted Credit is Suitable for Stateful Harness Self-Evolution ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
formally shows how discounting supports adaptive module selection under
evolving harness states by attenuating stale credit and restoring
exploration pressure for modules that have not been selected recently.

### IV-B Persistent Memory and Long-Horizon Feedback

Long-horizon AOD can produce hundreds or thousands of evaluated
candidates, making it impractical to expose the complete search history
to an LLM at every step. Moreover, retaining all records in external
storage does not imply that they remain effectively available to the
model. Finite context windows and repeated summarization can bias the
working context toward recent attempts. HEMO therefore separates
*persistent storage* from *effective retrieval* through an external
memory filesystem and explicit long-horizon feedback mechanisms.

Structured experience memory. The memory filesystem stores the search
experience of the evaluated operator candidates outside the transient
LLM context as structured optimization events. Each record can retain
candidate designs, evaluation results, parent information, validity or
failure information, Pareto-related status, operator context, and other
search metadata. This provides a persistent empirical history that
remains reusable across successive harness states.

Periodic long-term feedback. HEMO periodically transforms accumulated
search history into compact diagnostic feedback. These tools summarize
the evolving search trajectory and identify prolonged stagnation or
repeated search patterns, allowing subsequent harness modules to access
abstracted signals without rescanning the complete history. We refer to
each periodic invocation of these tools as a *heartbeat*, consisting
primarily of a summary report and a stagnation report, and the latest
report of each type is maintained as the only active reference record.

### IV-C MOCO-Specific Harness Design

HEMO separates its AOD harness into a fixed execution scaffold and a set
of evolvable decision roles. As shown in
Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization"),
the fixed scaffold preserves the AOD harness lifecycle, while the
evolvable roles capture decisions whose preferred behavior depends on
the current search state.

Fixed execution scaffold. Four operational interfaces remain fixed
throughout the entire stateful harness self-evolution process. 1)
Evaluation interface. It specifies solver configuration, dataset
generation, evaluation instances, and feedback construction
independently of the harness loop, preventing harness changes from
altering the evaluation protocol or gaming the intended objective. 2)
Multi-objective archive interface. It merges newly generated operator
candidates into the candidate Pareto archive using a fixed non-dominated
sorting rule, keeping Pareto filtering and diversity preservation
consistent throughout harness state transition. 3) Diagnostic and
heartbeat interface. It exposes standardized tools for summarizing the
search history and diagnosing stagnation patterns. The heartbeat tools
and callable interfaces remain fixed, while the decision modules
determine how the resulting diagnostic feedback is retrieved and
utilized. 4) Memory-writing interface. It records evaluated candidates
and search events using a common schema, ensuring a consistent empirical
history across successive harness states. This separates persistent
bookkeeping from the adaptive policy that determines which experience
becomes active context. Examples of evolved harness states and generated
operators are in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Seed and Evolved Harness Modules ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
and
 [J](#A10 "Appendix J Representative Discovered Heuristics and Operator Combinations ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

Evolvable decision roles. Within this scaffold, HEMO exposes four
high-level roles whose behavior can be modified by the harness state
transition.

Experience Retrieval. This role determines which historical candidate
records and reports of the previously discovered search patterns should
be surfaced from memory filesystem for the current AOD step. Its purpose
is not merely to compress context, but to decide adaptively which parts
of the long-horizon optimization history are currently useful.

Target Selection. When the underlying optimization solver exposes
multiple search components or evolutionary operators, this role
determines which component should receive the next design intervention.
Such a decision is particularly relevant to multi-component evolutionary
solvers such as NSGA-II \[[7](#bib.bib15)\], where the marginal value of
improving one operator depends on the current behavior of the
surrounding operators. For solvers with only one evolvable component,
this role can degenerate to a trivial choice and need not introduce
additional control complexity.

Parent Selection. This role selects previously evaluated candidates that
serve as reference parents for the next generation action. These parents
provide concrete working context from which the LLM can identify
reusable structures, compare patterns associated with success and
failures, and decide whether to refine an existing design or redirect
the search toward a different region.

Candidate Evolution. This role determines the search strategy used to
produce successive candidates within a bounded harness evaluation
episode. It controls how the search progresses from one evaluated
candidate to the next, coordinating candidate generation, evaluation,
and subsequent iterations. The resulting strategy may follow iterative,
population based, trajectory based, staged, or hybrid search behavior,
allowing HEMO to adapt the dynamics of candidate evolution.

Overall self-evolution procedure.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ IV-C MOCO-Specific Harness Design ‣ IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
summarizes the complete outer harness self-evolution procedure. To
support controlled comparison and cleaner credit assignment, each
harness evaluation initializes its local candidate population from the
same fixed seed pool. The Executor Agent returns the valid retained
candidates, their mean score vector containing negative HV and runtime,
and an execution trace. Successfully evaluated children update the
external harness and candidate Pareto archives, while their execution
records remain in memory even when they do not replace the current
harness.

1: Seed harness $`H_{\mathrm{seed}}`$; fixed seed pool
$`\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{seed}}`$; harness evaluation budget
$`B_{\mathrm{outer}}`$; per-harness candidate budget $`B_{H}`$

2: Notation: $`\mathbf{s}(H)`$ denotes the current harness score,
$`\mathbf{s}^{\prime}`$ the proposed harness score, $`\mathcal{V}`$ the
evaluated candidates returned by the executor, and $`\mathrm{ok}`$
evaluation success.

3: Initialize memory filesystem $`\mathcal{M}`$, harness archive
$`\mathcal{A}_{H}`$, and candidate archive $`\mathcal{A}_{A}`$

4: Generate initial harness states from $`H_{\mathrm{seed}}`$

5: Evaluate the seed and initial states using
$`(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{seed}},\mathcal{M},B_{H})`$

6: Update $`\mathcal{A}_{H}`$ and $`\mathcal{A}_{A}`$ with
initialization results

7: Sample current harness $`H`$ from $`\mathcal{A}_{H}`$

8: Initialize discounted UCB statistics for all evolvable modules

9: while harness evaluation budget remains do

10:   Select module $`m`$ using discounted UCB

11:   $`b\leftarrow\textsc{ProposerAgent}(H,m,\text{recent traces})`$
$`\triangleright`$ revise one module specification

12:   $`H^{\prime}\leftarrow\textsc{RealizerAgent}(H,m,b)`$
$`\triangleright`$ instantiate the proposed revision

13:
  $`(\mathcal{V},\mathbf{s}^{\prime},\mathrm{ok})\leftarrow\textsc{ExecutorAgent}(H^{\prime},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{seed}},\mathcal{M},B_{H})`$
$`\triangleright`$ run a bounded AOD episode

14:   if $`\mathrm{ok}`$ then

15:    Update Pareto archive $`\mathcal{A}_{A}`$ with $`\mathcal{V}`$

16:    Update Pareto archive $`\mathcal{A}_{H}`$ with
$`(H^{\prime},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})`$

17:    Compute reward $`r`$ from the relative improvement of
$`\mathbf{s}^{\prime}`$ over $`\mathbf{s}(H)`$ $`\triangleright`$ assign
credit to module $`m`$

18:    if $`\mathbf{s}(H)`$ does not dominate $`\mathbf{s}^{\prime}`$
then

19:      $`H\leftarrow H^{\prime}`$ $`\triangleright`$ retain child code
and blueprint

20:    end if

21:   else

22:    $`r\leftarrow-1`$ $`\triangleright`$ retain the parent after
repair retries fail

23:   end if

24:   Update discounted UCB statistics using module $`m`$ and reward
$`r`$

25: end while

26: return $`\mathcal{A}_{H},\mathcal{A}_{A},\mathcal{M}`$

Algorithm 1 Stateful Harness Self-Evolution in HEMO

## V Experiments

Benchmarks and generalization protocol. We evaluate HEMO on eight MOCO
tasks spanning four representative problem
families \[[36](#bib.bib19)\], covering knapsack, vehicle routing, TSP,
and scheduling. Here, TSP, KP, MDKP, CVRP, SPDP, and FJSP denote the
traveling salesman problem, knapsack problem, multi-dimensional knapsack
problem, capacitated vehicle routing problem, selective pickup and
delivery problem, and flexible job shop scheduling problem,
respectively. The prefixes Bi- and Tri- denote bi-objective and
tri-objective formulations, respectively. The source-to-target pairs are
Bi-TSP $`\rightarrow`$ Tri-TSP, Bi-KP $`\rightarrow`$ Bi-MDKP, Bi-CVRP
$`\rightarrow`$ Bi-SPDP, and Bi-FJSP $`\rightarrow`$ Tri-FJSP, where the
source task is used for in-distribution harness self-evolution and the
target task for intra-family cross-task generalization with the fixed
harness state. Synthetic problems are evaluated at multiple sizes, while
FJSP uses the Brandimarte benchmark \[[58](#bib.bib35)\] instances for
final evaluation. Detailed task formulations are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmark Problems ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

HEMO configuration. We instantiate HEMO with both
SEMO \[[35](#bib.bib18)\] and NSGA-II \[[7](#bib.bib15)\] as two
structurally distinct optimization backbones. Harness self-evolution
allows at most 200 harness state evaluations for both SEMO and NSGA-II.
Each SEMO harness evaluation generates 50 candidates with population
size 5, while each NSGA-II evaluation allows 100 complete operator
combination evaluations with operator and combination population sizes
of 10.

Objectives and evaluation metrics. During AOD, all generated operator
candidates are evaluated jointly by solution quality and computational
efficiency, represented by negative Hypervolume (HV) and runtime under a
common lower-is-better convention. Final performance is reported using
HV, runtime, and Inverted Generational Distance (IGD), where higher HV
and lower IGD indicate better Pareto-front coverage and smaller distance
to the reference Pareto front, respectively. Metric definitions,
reference points, and objective normalization are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

Compared baselines and evaluation protocol. We compare HEMO with three
groups of baselines: (1) Conventional MOEAs, including SEMO, NSGA-II,
MOEA/D \[[8](#bib.bib16)\], and PFG-MOEA \[[37](#bib.bib65)\], (2)
Neural MOCO methods, represented by PMOCO \[[9](#bib.bib23)\] and (3)
LLM-based AOD methods, including EoH \[[14](#bib.bib11)\],
MEoH \[[17](#bib.bib32)\], MPaGE \[[18](#bib.bib34)\], and
E2OC \[[19](#bib.bib36)\]. The HEMO Proposer, Realizer, and Executor
agents use Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5, and GPT-4.1-nano, respectively.
During inference, all LLM-based AOD methods use GPT-5-nano unless
otherwise stated, with identical candidate generation budgets of 2,000
for SEMO and 4,000 for NSGA-II and the same per-candidate evaluation
timeout. Unless otherwise stated, LLM-based AOD results are averaged
over four independent trials. For inference, initialization states are
excluded, and the evolved harness state with the smallest normalized
Euclidean distance to the empirical ideal point is selected from the
remaining harness states. The selected harness is then applied to both
the source task and its corresponding transfer task. For all MOEA
solvers, a uniform timeout of 3,600 seconds is imposed on each test run
across all test instances. Additional configuration and implementation
details are provided in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Experimental Details ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

Source-task performance with SEMO.
Table [I](#S5.T1 "TABLE I ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
reports the detailed results on the source tasks used during harness
self-evolution. HEMO achieves the highest HV in seven of the nine
task-size settings across Bi-TSP, Bi-CVRP, and Bi-KP. The advantage
becomes clearer on larger testing instances. For example, on Bi-CVRP
with $`N=100`$, HEMO reaches an HV of $`0.5700`$, compared with
$`0.5381`$ for the strongest baseline, while on Bi-KP with $`N=200`$ it
achieves $`0.3619`$ compared with $`0.3350`$. On Bi-TSP, the advantage
of HEMO becomes more pronounced as the problem size increases. These
results show that harness adaptation can further improve the quality of
generated heuristics over existing LLM-based AOD frameworks. Moreover,
the HV gains are not accompanied by consistently longer execution. HEMO
remains competitive in runtime and is the fastest method in several
larger settings, including Bi-TSP with $`N=100`$ and Bi-KP with
$`N=100`$ and $`N=200`$, suggesting that the improvement in solution
quality does not systematically come at the cost of higher heuristic
runtime.

Intra-family cross-task generalization.
Table [II](#S5.T2 "TABLE II ‣ V-A Main Results ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
evaluates the transferred harness in related target tasks. HEMO obtains
the best HV in five of nine settings and places second in the remaining
four. Although the target tasks are not seen during harness
self-evolution, the transferred harness remains competitive across all
three tasks. HEMO also achieves the fastest runtime among LLM-based AOD
methods in several transferred settings while consistently ranking first
in HV at the largest problem size, indicating that the learned harness
behavior can transfer effectively across related tasks. Additional FJSP
results with the SEMO backbone are provided in
Appendix [I-B](#A9.SS2 "I-B Additional Results with the SEMO Backbone ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization"),
while comparisons with expert-designed TSP operators and their
sequential combinations are provided in
Appendix [I-A](#A9.SS1 "I-A Comparison with Expert-Designed TSP Operators ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")

TSP.
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-A Main Results ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
directly compares HEMO with expert-designed operators and E2OC on Bi-TSP
and Tri-TSP. HEMO achieves the best HV and IGD in five of the six
settings, with E2OC only slightly ahead on Bi-TSP with $`N=20`$. On
Bi-TSP with $`N=50`$ and $`N=100`$, HEMO improves both reported metrics
over E2OC. Notably, the fixed transferred harness consistently achieves
the best HV and IGD at all three Tri-TSP sizes, indicating that the
evolved harness improves multi-operator design under NSGA-II and retains
its effectiveness when transferred from bi-objective to tri-objective
TSP.

FJSP.
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-A Main Results ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
further evaluates operator design on Bi-FJSP and Tri-FJSP. On Bi-FJSP,
HEMO achieves the highest HV for both ID and OOD instances and the best
overall HV and IGD. On Tri-FJSP, E2OC has a marginally higher HV on
Mk15, but HEMO obtains better HV and IGD on the OOD instances and
consequently the best overall solution quality. This pattern shows that
the evolved harness generalizes well across objective dimensionalities
and different machine and job configurations.
Appendix [I-C](#A9.SS3 "I-C Additional Results with the NSGA-II Backbone ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
reports NSGA-II results on knapsack and routing tasks.

### V-B Further Analysis

Comparison with a neural baseline. We compare the SEMO heuristics
evolved by HEMO (HEMO-SEMO) with PMOCO \[[9](#bib.bib23)\], a
preference-conditioned neural solver, across 16 (task, size)
combinations. Both methods are evaluated on the same 50 test instances
per setting, with consistent objective normalization and hypervolume
reference points. PMOCO uses the corresponding pretrained checkpoint
when available. For the larger TSP settings with $`N=150`$ and
$`N=200`$, we reuse its $`N=20`$ checkpoint without retraining. For
HEMO-SEMO, the compared heuristics are designed only on 10 IID instances
at a single design size for each problem family, as summarized in
Table [XIV](#A8.T14 "TABLE XIV ‣ H-B Harness Self-Evolution and Inference Protocols for HEMO and AOD Baselines ‣ Appendix H Experimental Details ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
in the appendix. The heuristic with the highest validation HV across all
runs is selected for reporting the test performance.

Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-B Further Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
shows that HEMO-SEMO achieves higher HV in 11 of 16 settings and lower
empirical IGD in 12 of 16 settings. It outperforms PMOCO on both metrics
across all Tri-TSP and Bi-KP settings, and also performs strongly on
Bi-TSP, including both larger problem sizes. Overall, HEMO with SEMO
achieves wins in more settings under both metrics, although the relative
advantage remains problem dependent.

The larger-size TSP results further examine cross-size generalization
beyond the task sizes used by the default pretrained configurations,
where generalization across problem sizes remains an important challenge
for neural MOCO methods \[[9](#bib.bib23)\]. On Bi-TSP, HEMO-SEMO
achieves higher HV and lower empirical IGD than PMOCO at both $`N=150`$
and $`N=200`$. The same pattern is observed on Tri-TSP, where HEMO-SEMO
also achieves higher HV and lower empirical IGD at both larger sizes.
Neural methods often require retraining on larger instances to improve
generalization across problem sizes. In contrast, HEMO with SEMO
outperforms PMOCO on both TSP tasks at $`N=150`$ and $`N=200`$ without
additional training, with both methods using the same training size.

Quality–runtime trade-offs.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V-B Further Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")(a)
shows how the heuristic-front HV evolves during inference. On the ID
tasks, Bi-TSP and Bi-CVRP, HEMO achieves the strongest final trade-offs
despite not always leading early, indicating the benefit of continued
refinement beyond the initial candidate population. On the OOD tasks,
Tri-TSP and Bi-SPDP, the trajectories are closer, but HEMO remains
competitive late in search and attains the highest final mean
heuristic-front HV, suggesting that effective search guidance persists
after intra-family transfer.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V-B Further Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")(b)
shows a complementary view of the final quality–runtime trade-offs. On
the ID tasks, HEMO covers favorable regions across quality levels, often
matching solution quality at lower runtime and offering alternatives for
different computational budgets rather than a single high-quality
candidate. On the OOD tasks, the fronts overlap more and no method
dominates every region, yet HEMO remains on or near the favorable
boundary across quality and runtime levels.

provides additional visualizations of the obtained solution sets.

We ablate the main components of HEMO on two TSP tasks under SEMO.
Table [V](#S5.T5 "TABLE V ‣ V-B Further Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
shows that the unevolved seed harness performs the worst, lowering HV by
$`0.3450`$ on Bi-TSP and $`0.3576`$ on Tri-TSP. Replacing the discounted
UCB with sequential module selection consistently worsens HV and IGD,
supporting adaptive credit assignment among the evolving decision
modules. Restricting memory access to records produced by the current
harness state further reduces performance, while removing the retrieved
memory context from subsequent search decisions causes an even larger
drop. These results indicate that the gains of HEMO arise jointly from
stateful harness self-evolution, adaptive module scheduling, and memory
filesystem, and that these benefits remain visible after cross-task
transfer.

Cost and performance across LLM backbones. We further evaluate HEMO with
different LLM backbones to examine the trade-off between search
performance and computational cost.
Table [VI](#S5.T6 "TABLE VI ‣ V-B Further Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
reports token consumption, API cost, wall-clock runtime, HV, and
empirical IGD on Bi-CVRP and its transferred Bi-SPDP task.

The comparison highlights a clear cost–performance trade-off across
different LLM backbones. GPT-4.1-nano is among the fastest and least
expensive models, but produces weaker final heuristic performance than
the stronger backbones. This motivates its use for high-volume candidate
generation during harness self-evolution, where a large number of
evaluations make inference speed and cost particularly important.

For inference with a fixed selected harness state, GPT-5-nano provides a
stronger overall balance between search quality and computational cost.
It achieves the best HV and IGD on Bi-CVRP while remaining substantially
less expensive to use than Claude Haiku 4.5 and the Qwen backbones. On
Bi-SPDP, several larger models obtain slightly better final solution
quality, but at considerably higher API cost or substantially longer
wall-clock runtime. We therefore use GPT-5-nano as the common inference
backbone for HEMO and all LLM-based AOD baselines in the main
experiments, providing a strong and relatively cost-efficient model
under a unified evaluation setting.

### V-C Limitations and Future Directions

Model accessibility. The Proposer and Realizer currently use proprietary
language models, making harness self-evolution dependent on external API
access and cost. Adapting smaller or open weight models to these roles,
potentially through distillation of successful harness design
trajectories, could make the framework more accessible.

Evaluation cost and cross-task memory transfer. Candidate evaluation
remains computationally demanding, as assessing a designed candidate
requires executing it on multiple problem instances. While HEMO reuses
accumulated memory within a task, our cross-task experiments transfer
the harness rather than the task-specific memory accumulated during
search. A promising extension is a transferable memory filesystem that
distinguishes reusable design knowledge from observations and evaluation
records specific to each task. Such a mechanism could reduce redundant
exploration and evaluation on new tasks, while requiring safeguards
against negative transfer from incompatible prior experience.

Generalization across tasks. Although HEMO-SEMO outperforms PMOCO in
several settings, including the larger size Bi-TSP and Tri-TSP
experiments, its advantage is not uniform across problem families. PMOCO
remains stronger on Bi-CVRP, indicating that the relative effectiveness
of the two approaches depends on the target problem. An important
direction is therefore to investigate how design datasets for operators
and evaluators can better support generalization across instance sizes
and distributions. In particular, more diverse design instances and
evaluation criteria that explicitly assess robustness to distribution
shifts may help produce more broadly transferable operators.

## VI Conclusion

We present HEMO, a stateful harness self-evolution framework for
LLM-based automatic operator design in multi-objective combinatorial
optimization. By adapting the harness itself through localized state
transitions while preserving long-term optimization experience in a
memory filesystem, HEMO enables search control to co-evolve with the
operator design process. Comparing against state-of-the-art LLM-based
AOD methods, HEMO achieves strong performance across diverse tasks and
two different evolutionary backbones, while also exhibiting effective
intra-family cross-task transfer. We believe HEMO opens a promising
direction in which the harness itself becomes a persistent and adaptive
optimization object, enabling more effective long-horizon and
transferable operator design.
````
