````math
## Appendix Contents

## Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics

We evaluate the quality of the Pareto-front approximations using two
widely adopted multi-objective optimization metrics, namely Hypervolume
(HV) and Inverted Generational Distance (IGD). Both metrics jointly
reflect convergence toward high-quality trade-off solutions and the
coverage of the obtained Pareto front, but evaluate these properties
from different perspectives. Higher HV and lower IGD indicate better
performance.

### A-A Hypervolume

Hypervolume. Given a non-dominated objective set
$`P=\{\mathbf{y}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}^{K}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{M}`$ and
a reference point $`\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{M})^{\top}`$ that is
dominated by all points of interest under the minimization convention,
the Hypervolume (HV) measures the volume of the objective-space region
dominated by $`P`$ and bounded by $`\mathbf{r}`$. Formally,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{HV}_{\mathbf{r}}(P)=\lambda_{M}\left(\bigcup_{\mathbf{y}\in P}[y_{1},r_{1}]\times\cdots\times[y_{M},r_{M}]\right),
``` |  | (8) |

where $`\lambda_{M}(\cdot)`$ denotes the $`M`$-dimensional Lebesgue
measure.

HV simultaneously rewards convergence and diversity because solutions
closer to the Pareto front extend the dominated region toward better
objective values, while well-distributed non-dominated solutions cover a
broader region of the objective space. Therefore, a larger HV value
indicates a better Pareto-front approximation.

Because different MOCOPs can have substantially different objective
scales, making direct comparison across problem settings difficult, we
report normalized HV. Given an ideal point
$`\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{M})^{\top}`$, the normalized HV is
computed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{HV}^{\prime}_{\mathbf{r}}(P)=\frac{\mathrm{HV}_{\mathbf{r}}(P)}{\prod_{m=1}^{M}|r_{m}-z_{m}|}.
``` |  | (9) |

The same reference and ideal points are used for all compared methods on
a given benchmark setting. Their construction and the values used for
each problem are detailed in
Appendix [A-C](#A1.SS3 "A-C Objective Normalization and Reference Points ‣ Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

### A-B Inverted Generational Distance

Inverted Generational Distance. IGD evaluates an approximation from the
perspective of a reference Pareto front. Let $`Q`$ denote a reference
set representing the target Pareto front and let $`P`$ denote the
non-dominated set obtained by an algorithm. IGD is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{IGD}(P,Q)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in Q}\min_{\mathbf{p}\in P}\left\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\right\|_{2},
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\|\cdot\|_{2}`$ denotes Euclidean distance.

For every point on the reference front, IGD measures the distance to its
closest solution in the approximation and then averages these distances
over the entire reference front. Consequently, a low IGD requires both
good convergence and sufficient coverage, since an approximation
concentrated in only a small region of the Pareto front will retain
large distances to uncovered reference points. Lower IGD is therefore
better.

When an exact Pareto front is unavailable, we construct the reference
front from the union of the solution sets produced by all compared
methods and retain the non-dominated subset. The same reference front is
then used to evaluate every method under the corresponding benchmark
setting.

### A-C Objective Normalization and Reference Points

All objectives are represented under a minimization convention before
metric computation. We use fixed problem-specific and size-specific
reference and ideal points, as listed in
Table [VII](#A1.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ A-C Objective Normalization and Reference Points ‣ Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").
These points are shared by the compared methods within each setting.

|          |      |                                |                            |
|----------|------|--------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Problem  | Size | Reference point $`\mathbf{r}`$ | Ideal point $`\mathbf{z}`$ |
| Bi-KP    | 50   | $`(-5,-5)`$                    | $`(-30,-30)`$              |
|          | 100  | $`(-20,-20)`$                  | $`(-50,-50)`$              |
|          | 200  | $`(-30,-30)`$                  | $`(-75,-75)`$              |
| Bi-MDKP  | 50   | $`(-5,-5)`$                    | $`(-30,-30)`$              |
|          | 100  | $`(-20,-20)`$                  | $`(-50,-50)`$              |
|          | 200  | $`(-30,-30)`$                  | $`(-85,-85)`$              |
| Bi-CVRP  | 20   | $`(30,8)`$                     | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 50   | $`(45,8)`$                     | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 100  | $`(80,8)`$                     | $`(0,0)`$                  |
| Bi-SPDP  | 20   | $`(31.1,68.2)`$                | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 50   | $`(77.8,160.6)`$               | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 100  | $`(155.6,325.6)`$              | $`(0,0)`$                  |
| Bi-TSP   | 20   | $`(20,20)`$                    | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 50   | $`(35,35)`$                    | $`(0,0)`$                  |
|          | 100  | $`(65,65)`$                    | $`(0,0)`$                  |
| Tri-TSP  | 20   | $`(20,20,20)`$                 | $`(0,0,0)`$                |
|          | 50   | $`(35,35,35)`$                 | $`(0,0,0)`$                |
|          | 100  | $`(65,65,65)`$                 | $`(0,0,0)`$                |
| Bi-FJSP  | All  | $`(1.1,1.1)`$                  | $`(0,0)`$                  |
| Tri-FJSP | All  | $`(1.1,1.1,1.1)`$              | $`(0,0,0)`$                |

TABLE VII: Reference points and ideal points for the MOCOP benchmarks.

FJSP objective normalization. For Bi-FJSP and Tri-FJSP, raw objective
values are divided by an instance-specific scale determined from
processing times, independently of the solutions produced by the
compared methods. For instance $`I`$, this scale is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S_{I}=\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}_{I}}\max_{k\in\mathcal{M}_{o}}p_{ok},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\mathcal{O}_{I}`$ is the set of operations, $`\mathcal{M}_{o}`$
contains the eligible machines for operation $`o`$, and $`p_{ok}`$ is
its processing time on machine $`k`$. The normalized objectives are

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       f^{\prime}_{m}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{f_{m}(\mathbf{x})}{S_{I}}.
       ```                                                          |     | (12) |

In this normalized objective space, we use the ideal point
$`\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{0}`$ and the HV reference point

|     |                                         |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbf{r}^{*}=(1.1,\ldots,1.1)^{\top},
       ```                                      |     | (13) |

with two components for Bi-FJSP and three for Tri-FJSP. This scaling
does not use empirical ideal or nadir points estimated from the compared
methods’ solution fronts.

Other benchmarks and HV scaling. For the knapsack, routing, and
traveling salesman benchmarks, HV is computed using the fixed reference
and ideal points in
Table [VII](#A1.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ A-C Objective Normalization and Reference Points ‣ Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").
The reported HV is normalized by the reference box volume:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{HV}_{\mathrm{norm}}(\mathcal{P})=\frac{\mathrm{HV}(\mathcal{P};\mathbf{r})}{\prod_{m=1}^{M}(r_{m}-z_{m})},
``` |  | (14) |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$, $`\mathbf{r}`$, and $`\mathbf{z}`$ are expressed
in the same objective space.

## Appendix B Benchmark Problems

We evaluate HEMO on eight multi-objective combinatorial optimization
tasks spanning four well-studied families, covering *knapsack*,
*routing*, *traveling salesman*, and *scheduling*. These families are
among the most extensively studied classes of MOCOPs in the evolutionary
optimization literature \[[36](#bib.bib19)\]. For each family, one task
is used for harness self-evolution and a related task for intra-family
cross-task generalization, with source-to-target pairs of Bi-KP to
Bi-MDKP, Bi-CVRP to Bi-SPDP, Bi-TSP to Tri-TSP, and Bi-FJSP to Tri-FJSP.
The benchmark configuration is summarized in
Table [VIII](#A2.T8 "TABLE VIII ‣ Appendix B Benchmark Problems ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").
Detailed harness self-evolution and inference settings are provided in
Appendix [H-B](#A8.SS2 "H-B Harness Self-Evolution and Inference Protocols for HEMO and AOD Baselines ‣ Appendix H Experimental Details ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Family | Problem |  Objectives | Final test instances |
| Knapsack | Bi-KP |  two collected profits | $`n\in\{50,100,200\}`$ |
| Knapsack | Bi-MDKP |  two collected profits | $`n\in\{50,100,200\}`$ |
| Routing | Bi-CVRP |  total distance; longest route | $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$ |
| Routing | Bi-SPDP |  total distance; required vehicle capacity | $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$ |
| TSP | Bi-TSP |  two tour lengths | $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$ |
| TSP | Tri-TSP |  three tour lengths | $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$ |
| Scheduling | Bi-FJSP |  makespan; maximum machine load | Mk01–Mk15 |
| Scheduling | Tri-FJSP |  makespan; maximum machine load; total machine load | Mk01–Mk15 |

TABLE VIII: Overview of the MOCOP benchmarks used in our experiments.
Each synthetic problem size contains $`50`$ fixed test instances. For
FJSP, Mk15 is used during operator design for NSGA-II, while all 15
Brandimarte instances are used for final evaluation.

### B-A Knapsack Problems

Bi-objective Knapsack Problem (Bi-KP). The bi-objective knapsack problem
extends the classical $`0`$–$`1`$ knapsack problem by associating each
item with two profit values. Given $`n`$ items, let $`w_{i}`$ denote the
weight of item $`i`$, and let $`p_{i}^{(1)}`$ and $`p_{i}^{(2)}`$ denote
its profits under the two objectives. A solution is represented by a
binary vector $`\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}`$, where $`x_{i}=1`$ indicates
that item $`i`$ is selected. The problem is formulated as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(1)}x_{i},\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(2)}x_{i}\right),
``` |  | (15) |

subject to

|     |                                 |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}x_{i}\leq C,
       ```                              |     | (16) |

where $`C`$ denotes the knapsack capacity.

The two optimization backbones use different numerical coefficient
scales for Bi-KP. In the SEMO implementation, the weights $`w_{i}`$ and
the two profits $`p_{i}^{(1)}`$ and $`p_{i}^{(2)}`$ are sampled
independently from $`\operatorname{Unif}[0,1)`$. The capacity follows

|     |                                      |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C=\begin{cases}12.5,&50\leq n<100,\\
       25.0,&100\leq n\leq 200.\end{cases}
       ```                                   |     | (17) |

Thus, the tested instances use capacities $`12.5`$, $`25`$, and $`25`$
for $`n=50`$, $`100`$, and $`200`$, respectively.

In the NSGA-II implementation, the weights and both profits are sampled
independently from the discrete uniform distribution
$`\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,100\}`$, and the capacity is determined
from the generated weights as

|     |                                                     |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C=\left\lfloor 0.5\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\right\rfloor.
       ```                                                  |     | (18) |

Both implementations are evaluated at $`n\in\{50,100,200\}`$, using
$`50`$ fixed test instances for each size.

Bi-objective Multi-dimensional Knapsack Problem (Bi-MDKP). Bi-MDKP
generalizes Bi-KP by introducing multiple resource
constraints \[[3](#bib.bib52)\]. Each item $`i`$ has two profits
$`p_{i}^{(1)}`$ and $`p_{i}^{(2)}`$ and consumes $`w_{ji}`$ units of
resource $`j`$. With $`m`$ resource constraints, the problem is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(1)}x_{i},\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(2)}x_{i}\right),
``` |  | (19) |

subject to

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ji}x_{i}\leq C_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
       ```                                                       |     | (20) |

We use $`m=5`$ resource constraints and a tightness factor $`\tau=0.5`$.

In the SEMO implementation, all resource consumptions $`w_{ji}`$ and
profits $`p_{i}^{(1)},p_{i}^{(2)}`$ are independently sampled from
$`\operatorname{Unif}[0,1)`$, and the capacity of each resource is

|     |                                                         |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{j}=\tau\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ji}=0.5\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ji}.
       ```                                                      |     | (21) |

In the NSGA-II implementation, the resource consumptions and profits are
independently sampled from $`\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,100\}`$, with

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{j}=\left\lfloor\tau\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ji}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor 0.5\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ji}\right\rfloor.
``` |  | (22) |

We evaluate Bi-MDKP at $`n\in\{50,100,200\}`$, using $`50`$ fixed test
instances for each size. The formulation follows the standard
bi-objective multi-dimensional knapsack setting \[[59](#bib.bib53)\].

### B-B Routing Problems

Bi-objective Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (Bi-CVRP). Bi-CVRP
considers one depot and $`n`$ customer nodes. Each customer $`i`$ has a
demand $`d_{i}`$, and a homogeneous fleet of vehicles with capacity
$`Q`$ must serve every customer exactly once. Each route starts and ends
at the depot, and the total demand assigned to a route cannot exceed
$`Q`$. Given a set of routes $`\mathcal{R}`$, we minimize

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{1}(\mathcal{R})=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\mathrm{len}(r),\qquad f_{2}(\mathcal{R})=\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\mathrm{len}(r).
``` |  | (23) |

The first objective measures total routing cost, whereas the second
penalizes disproportionately long individual routes and therefore
encourages workload balance among vehicles.

For every instance, depot and customer coordinates are sampled
independently and uniformly from $`[0,1)^{2}`$, and customer demands are
sampled independently from $`\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,9\}`$.
Vehicle capacities are set to $`Q=30`$, $`40`$, and $`50`$ for $`n=20`$,
$`50`$, and $`100`$, respectively. We evaluate $`50`$ fixed instances at
each size $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$.

Bi-objective Selective Pickup and Delivery Problem (Bi-SPDP). Bi-SPDP
jointly minimizes travel distance and required vehicle
capacity \[[60](#bib.bib64)\]. A single vehicle starts and ends at a
depot, visits every delivery node, and selects a subset of pickup nodes
that supplies the required commodities. Pickups and deliveries are not
paired, so commodities collected at any pickup node can satisfy any
subsequent delivery.

Let $`q_{i}>0`$ denote the supply at a pickup node and $`q_{i}<0`$ the
signed demand at a delivery node, with $`q_{0}=0`$ at the depot. For a
route $`\pi=(0,\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m},0)`$, define the vehicle load
after the $`k`$th visit as

|     |                                                 |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}q_{\pi_{j}},\qquad L_{0}=0.
       ```                                              |     | (24) |

A feasible route visits each selected node once, includes all delivery
nodes, and satisfies $`L_{k}\geq 0`$ throughout the route. The two
minimization objectives are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{1}(\pi)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\|\mathbf{c}_{\pi_{k+1}}-\mathbf{c}_{\pi_{k}}\|_{2},\qquad f_{2}(\pi)=\max_{0\leq k\leq m}L_{k},
``` |  | (25) |

where $`\pi_{0}=\pi_{m+1}=0`$ and $`\mathbf{c}_{i}`$ denotes node
coordinates. Thus, vehicle capacity is an objective determined by the
maximum route load, not a fixed capacity constraint.

We construct synthetic instances of this formulation using our own
generator. Here, size $`n`$ counts all nodes, including the depot.
Coordinates are sampled independently and uniformly from $`[0,1)^{2}`$.
The $`n-1`$ non-depot nodes are randomly partitioned into
$`\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor`$ pickup nodes and the remaining delivery nodes.
Pickup supplies are sampled uniformly from $`\{1,\ldots,9\}`$ and
delivery demand magnitudes from $`\{1,\ldots,6\}`$. If total supply is
insufficient, pickup supplies are incremented one unit at a time in
round-robin order until they cover total demand. We generate $`50`$
fixed test instances for each $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$.

For each size, the test reference point is
$`(1.1n\sqrt{2},\,1.1S_{n})`$, where $`S_{n}`$ is the largest total
pickup supply among its test instances. The ideal point is $`(0,0)`$.
The Bi-SPDP reference points in
Table [VII](#A1.T7 "TABLE VII ‣ A-C Objective Normalization and Reference Points ‣ Appendix A Multi-Objective Performance Metrics ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
are rounded to one decimal place for presentation only. Evaluation uses
the full-precision reference points stored with the instances.

### B-C Traveling Salesman Problems

Bi-objective and Tri-objective TSP. The multi-objective traveling
salesman problem (MOTSP) requires a Hamiltonian tour that visits every
city exactly once and returns to its starting city. We follow the
commonly used synthetic Euclidean MOTSP construction in which each
objective is associated with an independent two-dimensional coordinate
space \[[61](#bib.bib27)\].

For an $`M`$-objective instance, city $`i`$ is associated with

|     |                                                       |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbf{c}^{(m)}_{i}\in[0,1)^{2},\qquad m=1,\ldots,M,
       ```                                                    |     | (26) |

where all coordinates are sampled independently. The edge cost under
objective $`m`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{ij}^{(m)}=\left\|\mathbf{c}^{(m)}_{i}-\mathbf{c}^{(m)}_{j}\right\|_{2}.
``` |  | (27) |

For a tour $`\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n})`$, its objective value is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{m}(\pi)=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}d_{\pi_{k},\pi_{k+1}}^{(m)}+d_{\pi_{n},\pi_{1}}^{(m)}.
``` |  | (28) |

Bi-TSP uses $`M=2`$ independent coordinate spaces, while Tri-TSP uses
$`M=3`$. Hence, one instance can equivalently be represented by
coordinates in $`[0,1)^{4}`$ and $`[0,1)^{6}`$, respectively. We
evaluate both variants at $`n\in\{20,50,100\}`$, with $`50`$ fixed test
instances at each size.

### B-D Scheduling Problems

Bi-objective and Tri-objective Flexible Job Shop Scheduling. The
flexible job shop scheduling problem (FJSP) consists of a set of jobs,
each containing an ordered sequence of operations. Unlike the standard
job shop scheduling problem, each operation can be processed by one of
several eligible machines, with a potentially different processing time
on each machine. Operations belonging to the same job must satisfy their
precedence constraints, and each machine can process at most one
operation at any time.

Following established multi-objective FJSP
formulations \[[62](#bib.bib25), [63](#bib.bib26)\], we use three common
scheduling objectives. Let $`C_{j}`$ denote the completion time of job
$`j`$, and let $`L_{k}`$ denote the total processing load assigned to
machine $`k`$. We define

|     |                         |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{\max}=\max_{j}C_{j},
       ```                      |     | (29) |

|     |                         |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L_{\max}=\max_{k}L_{k},
       ```                      |     | (30) |

and

|     |                                 |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_{k}L_{k}.
       ```                              |     | (31) |

Bi-FJSP minimizes $`(C_{\max},L_{\max})`$, whereas Tri-FJSP minimizes
$`(C_{\max},L_{\max},L_{\mathrm{sum}})`$.

For SEMO, heuristic design uses 15 synthetic FJSP instances, each with
20 jobs and a machine count in $`\{5,10,15\}`$. Each job contains 2 to
10 operations, each operation is eligible for 1 to 5 machines, and
processing times are sampled uniformly from the integers 1 to 99. For
NSGA-II, operator design instead uses the Brandimarte instance Mk15.
Consequently, all Brandimarte instances are out of distribution for
SEMO, whereas Mk15 is in distribution and Mk01–Mk14 are held out for
NSGA-II.

The held-out FJSP test suite therefore covers $`n\in\{10,15,20,30\}`$
jobs and machine counts ranging from $`4`$ to $`15`$. Compared with the
knapsack and routing families, FJSP also introduces a qualitatively
different decision structure in which each candidate jointly determines
an operation sequence and a machine assignment while satisfying
precedence and machine-capacity constraints.

## Appendix C Multi-Objective Optimization Backbones

HEMO is evaluated with two multi-objective evolutionary backbones, SEMO
and NSGA-II, which expose substantially different search structures and
operator design spaces. This section describes their procedures and
experimental configurations, and discusses why both backbones are
considered.

### C-A SEMO

Simple Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization (SEMO) is a minimalist
Pareto-based evolutionary algorithm that maintains a set of mutually
non-dominated solutions \[[35](#bib.bib18)\]. Let $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$
denote the Pareto archive at iteration $`t`$. Each SEMO iteration
consists of the following steps:

1.  1.
    Parent selection. A solution $`\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ is
    selected from the current archive.
2.  2.
    Variation. A problem-specific mutation or neighborhood operator is
    applied to $`\mathbf{x}`$ to produce a candidate solution
    $`\mathbf{x}^{\prime}`$.
3.  3.
    Evaluation. The candidate is checked for feasibility and its
    multi-objective fitness vector $`\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})`$
    is evaluated.
4.  4.
    Pareto archive update. If $`\mathbf{x}^{\prime}`$ is dominated by an
    existing archive member, it is rejected. Otherwise,
    $`\mathbf{x}^{\prime}`$ is inserted and all solutions dominated by
    it are removed.

The archive update can be expressed compactly as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{P}_{t+1}=\mathrm{ND}\left(\mathcal{P}_{t}\cup\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\}\right),
``` |  | (32) |

where $`\mathrm{ND}(\cdot)`$ denotes the non-dominated subset.

SEMO is particularly suitable for HEMO for several reasons. First, its
deliberately simple control structure limits manually engineered
population-management mechanisms, making changes induced by the AOD
harness easier to isolate. Second, SEMO follows a lightweight
incremental update in which only one offspring is generated and
evaluated at each iteration. This is especially attractive for harness
evaluation, where each generated heuristic must be executed repeatedly
across optimization instances. The original analysis of SEMO also shows
that, despite its simplicity, it can achieve running time of the same
order as a multistart $`(1+1)`$-EA on the studied bi-objective model
problems  \[[35](#bib.bib18)\]. Third, SEMO maintains a variable-size
archive containing the nondominated solutions discovered so far, without
requiring a fixed population size or additional environmental selection.
This provides a direct representation of the evolving trade-offs while
keeping the underlying solver mechanics minimal.

In our implementation, each SEMO run is initialized with $`100`$
randomly generated feasible solutions. Candidate solutions are then
generated and evaluated sequentially, with the Pareto archive updated
after every iteration. We distinguish the relatively small search budget
used to evaluate candidates during harness self-evolution from the
substantially larger budget used for final evaluation.
Table [IX](#A3.T9 "TABLE IX ‣ C-A SEMO ‣ Appendix C Multi-Objective Optimization Backbones ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
summarizes these settings.

|          |              |              |            |            |
|----------|--------------|--------------|------------|------------|
| Problem  | Design init. | Design steps | Test init. | Test steps |
| Bi-KP    | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 10,000     |
| Bi-MDKP  | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 10,000     |
| Bi-CVRP  | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 10,000     |
| Bi-SPDP  | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 20,000     |
| Bi-TSP   | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 20,000     |
| Tri-TSP  | 100          | 2,000        | 100        | 20,000     |
| Bi-FJSP  | 100          | 750          | 100        | 15,000     |
| Tri-FJSP | 100          | 750          | 100        | 15,000     |

TABLE IX: SEMO initialization and iteration budgets. “Design” denotes
evaluation of candidates during harness self-evolution and inference of
HEMO, whereas “test” denotes final evaluation of the selected
candidates.

### C-B NSGA-II

NSGA-II is an elitist, population-based multi-objective evolutionary
algorithm \[[7](#bib.bib15)\]. Its design combines non-dominated sorting
with diversity preservation through crowding distance. Unlike SEMO,
which accepts or rejects every candidate immediately, NSGA-II collects
an entire offspring population before performing environmental selection
at the generation level.

Given a parent population $`P_{t}`$ of size $`N`$, one generation
proceeds as follows:

1.  1.
    Parent selection. Parent solutions are selected by tournament
    selection. For the knapsack, routing, and TSP implementations,
    tournament fitness is determined by non-dominated rank. In the FJSP
    implementation, rank remains the primary criterion and crowding
    distance is used to break ties in favor of solutions located in less
    populated regions of objective space.
2.  2.
    Variation. Problem-specific crossover and mutation operators are
    applied to the selected parents to construct an offspring population
    $`Q_{t}`$.
3.  3.
    Population merging. The current parent population and its offspring
    are combined:

    |     |                        |     |      |
    |-----|------------------------|-----|------|
    |     |
           ``` math
           R_{t}=P_{t}\cup Q_{t}.
           ```                     |     | (33) |
4.  4.
    Non-dominated sorting. The combined population is partitioned into
    successive non-dominated fronts

    |     |                     |     |      |
    |-----|---------------------|-----|------|
    |     |
           ``` math
           F_{1},F_{2},\ldots,
           ```                  |     | (34) |

    where $`F_{1}`$ contains the non-dominated members of $`R_{t}`$,
    $`F_{2}`$ contains the non-dominated members after removing
    $`F_{1}`$, and so forth.
5.  5.
    Crowding-distance estimation. Within each front, crowding distance
    estimates the density of neighboring solutions in objective space.
    For an interior solution $`\mathbf{x}`$, it is computed as

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    d(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{f_{m}(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{next}})-f_{m}(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{prev}})}{f_{m}^{\max}-f_{m}^{\min}},
    ``` |  |

    where $`\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{prev}}`$ and
    $`\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{next}}`$ are the neighboring solutions after
    sorting the front by objective $`m`$. Boundary solutions are
    assigned infinite crowding distance. Larger values therefore
    indicate less densely populated regions and are preferred when
    diversity must be preserved.
6.  6.
    Environmental selection. Complete fronts are inserted into the next
    population $`P_{t+1}`$ in increasing Pareto-rank order. If the next
    front cannot be accommodated in full, the remaining population slots
    are filled by selecting the solutions with the largest crowding
    distances from that front.

These components, including non-dominated sorting, elitist preservation,
crowding distance, and selection, constitute the central control
mechanisms of NSGA-II \[[36](#bib.bib19)\]. Compared with SEMO, NSGA-II
therefore exposes a richer set of interactions at the population level
and delays the effect of individual variation decisions until
environmental selection at the end of a generation.

In our implementation, the standard NSGA-II population management
procedure remains fixed, whereas the task-specific variation operators
exposed to the LLM constitute the inner operator design space. We
distinguish three evaluation stages, namely harness self-evolution,
inference with the selected harness, and final testing. During harness
self-evolution, we use small populations and short generation budgets to
compare harness states at low computational cost. During inference, both
the population size and generation budget are doubled to evaluate
candidate operator combinations more thoroughly and improve the
resolution of their quality–runtime comparisons. For example, a
population size of 50 and a generation budget of 15 become 100 and 30,
respectively. These larger solver budgets allow differences between
candidate operator combinations to emerge over a more substantial
optimization process. Final testing uses separate budgets to assess the
selected operators.

| kp_bitflip |  Mutate binary item-selection decisions by choosing which items to include or exclude. Weights, both objective profits, and capacity information can guide the selection and extent of these changes. |
| kp_crossover |  Recombine binary item-selection vectors across individuals, controlling pairing and inheritance of item choices. The reference operator uses uniform crossover. |
| kp_repair_mutation |  Repair or locally improve an item subset through selective item removal and insertion, balancing resource consumption against objective profits. The design accounts for a single capacity in KP or multiple resource capacities in MDKP. |
| operation_crossover |  Recombine operation-priority random keys across individuals to alter the decoded operation sequence, preserving $`[0,1]`$ bounds and leaving machine-option genes unchanged. |
| operation_mutation |  Perturb operation-priority random keys to alter the decoded sequence, controlling key selection and perturbation magnitude while preserving $`[0,1]`$ bounds and leaving machine-option genes unchanged. |
| machine_crossover |  Recombine machine-option genes across individuals to alter operation assignments, preserving eligible integer option indices and leaving operation-priority keys unchanged. |
| machine_mutation |  Change selected machine-option genes to eligible alternatives, controlling which operations are reassigned and to which machines while preserving valid option indices and leaving operation-priority keys unchanged. |

Representation-specific constraints. For Bi-CVRP, operators receive
customer demands, vehicle capacity, and distances and modify customer
permutations without depot markers. The fixed decoder inserts depot
visits and splits the giant tour according to vehicle capacity. For
Bi-SPDP, operators modify signed node permutations: absolute node
identifiers specify the visit order, while pickup node signs encode
inclusion or omission. For Bi-KP and Bi-MDKP, the same operator names
act on binary vectors, using a single capacity or multiple resource
capacities, respectively. A separate fixed feasibility repair is applied
after the operator sequence, independently of the designed
kp_repair_mutation implementation.

For TSP and FJSP, the representations and operator role decomposition
follow E2OC \[[19](#bib.bib36)\]. More specifically, for TSP, the three
operator interfaces, tsp_oropt, tsp_2opt, and tsp_3opt, act sequentially
on the same offspring permutation matrix. Their seed implementations
perform segment relocation, segment reversal, and multi-segment
rearrangement, respectively. Generated operators may redesign these
transformations while preserving the matrix shape and a complete city
permutation in each row. For FJSP, the chromosome contains two blocks,
namely continuous operation-priority keys and discrete machine-option
indices. The decoder selects the operation with the lowest priority key
among the next unscheduled operations of all jobs and schedules it
subject to job precedence and machine availability. The four interfaces
separate sequencing and assignment decisions, with crossover and
mutation provided for each block.

### C-C Why Two Backbones?

SEMO and NSGA-II differ in both evolutionary control and the structure
of the operator design problem exposed to HEMO. SEMO performs an
incremental Pareto archive update after every candidate evaluation,
producing a tightly coupled loop between candidate generation and
acceptance. NSGA-II instead evaluates variation through a generational
population process with non-dominated sorting and diversity
preservation, introducing delayed interactions at the population level.

The two backbones also represent different levels of algorithmic
composition. Under SEMO, the AOD process primarily evolves a single
problem-specific neighborhood operator that determines how candidate
solutions are generated from the current archive. Under NSGA-II, the
solver contains multiple evolvable operators whose effects depend on the
surrounding operator configuration. The harness must therefore
additionally decide which component to improve and reason about
interactions among operator candidates.

These differences in solver structure and design granularity also change
the information available to the AOD harness. Under SEMO, the harness
can reason over a persistent non-dominated archive and the direct
consequence of individual neighborhood moves. Under NSGA-II, it must
additionally account for interactions at the population level, multiple
variation operators, and the delayed effect of environmental selection.
Evaluating HEMO under both settings tests whether a stateful AOD harness
can adapt effectively across both single-operator and multi-operator
design, as well as across substantially different evolutionary control
structures. This reduces the risk that the learned harness behavior is
specific to the idiosyncrasies of one solver architecture.

## Appendix D Algorithmic Details of HEMO

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ IV-C MOCO-Specific Harness Design ‣ IV Methodology ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
in the main paper presents the outer harness self-evolution procedure.
This section provides the backbone-specific execution contracts for SEMO
and NSGA-II.

We distinguish bounded internal populations from external Pareto
archives. $`\operatorname{Select}_{K}`$ performs non-dominated sorting,
retains successive fronts up to capacity $`K`$, and uses descending
crowding distance to truncate the first front that does not fit. In
contrast, external Pareto archives retain all unique non-dominated
entries without capacity truncation. Internal populations may therefore
contain multiple dominance fronts.

The harness comprises four decision modules, with retrieve_memory
retrieving relevant search experience and select_target_algorithm
selecting the operator component to improve, while
select_parent_algorithm selects reference implementations and
evolve_target_algorithm controls candidate evolution within a bounded
evaluation budget. Under SEMO, the target is a complete heuristic, so
target operator selection is fixed and the remaining three modules are
evolvable. Under NSGA-II, the target is an individual operator within a
combination, and all four modules are evolvable.

Algorithm 3 NSGA-II Harness Execution

Under NSGA-II,
Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix D Algorithmic Details of HEMO ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
uses fixed orchestration to allocate a bounded episode to
evolve_target_algorithm, which returns the number of attempts consumed.
Each attempt uses a fixed helper to generate an operator with the
Executor Agent, evaluate it, and record the outcome, with the latter two
steps detailed in EvaluateCandidate. Only the selected operator is
replaced, and its score is measured in the resulting complete
combination, with the accompanying operator identities retained as
evaluation context.

The fixed rule for updating the current combination accepts a valid
candidate if it dominates the current combination or survives population
selection. Otherwise, acceptance depends on the mean relative score
change, with a decreasing temperature making the rule more selective as
the search progresses. Finalization returns the valid retained
combinations and their mean score, with the valid current combination as
a fallback.

## Appendix E Prompts

We present the user prompt templates for harness design, harness code
realization, inner heuristic generation, and diagnostic tool calls. We
use the prompts for SEMO to illustrate harness self-evolution and
heuristic generation. Repeated context, detailed fixed-call protocols,
API safeguards, and output boilerplate are explicitly marked where
omitted. Complete user prompts and system prompts, seed implementations
and the corresponding prompts for the NSGA-II backbone are provided in
the supplementary materials.

The prompts for generating blueprints of retrieve memory, select parent
algorithm, and evolve target algorithm module prepend the following
shared context. It is reproduced once here and explicitly omitted from
the three boxes.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E-A Evolvable Harness-Module Prompts

The module-specific prompts guide the Proposer Agent in constructing a
replacement blueprint for one decision module. The retrieve_memory
prompt specifies how to select compact empirical evidence, including
complementary trade-offs and failure patterns, while
select_target_algorithm selects which operator to evolve next in
multi-operator MOEAs. The select_parent_algorithm prompt specifies how
to choose diverse reference implementations, and evolve_target_algorithm
defines how to organize candidate search within its budget. Each
blueprint states the module’s goal, signature, decision logic, and local
hyperparameters. SEMO exposes a single heuristic target, making target
selection trivial, so the three remaining module prompts are shown
below.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E-B Harness Initialization and Code-Realization Prompts

The initialization prompt requests a complete harness blueprint that
coordinates the retrieve memory, select parent algorithm, and evolve
target algorithm modules. It encourages alternatives to the seed
strategy while requiring concrete local hyperparameters and
compatibility with the fixed runtime interfaces. The placeholders
\_\_PROMPT_FOR_MODULE_1\_\_, \_\_PROMPT_FOR_MODULE_2\_\_, and
\_\_PROMPT_FOR_MODULE_3\_\_ are replaced at runtime by the complete
module prompts, whose abridged versions appear above.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Realizer Agent converts blueprints into executable Python methods.
The complete harness prompt implements all evolvable modules during
initialization, whereas the single module prompt implements a proposed
replacement using the current code and harness blueprint as context.
Both constrain edits to the designated modules, preserve compatible
interfaces, and require explicit local parameter values, leaving the
fixed infrastructure unchanged.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E-C Inner Heuristic Generation Prompt

The inner generation prompt produces one candidate heuristic from the
task description and function template, selected parent implementations,
retrieved empirical records, and any diagnostic feedback. The harness
supplies generation guidance, while the Executor Agent chooses a
concrete design using this evidence. The prompt preserves the required
interface and feasibility constraints, discourages excessive runtime
overhead, and requests executable code alongside a short
natural-language description for memory recording.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E-D Memory Summary and Stagnation Report Prompts

The heartbeat invokes two diagnostic tools to turn retrieved experience
into feedback for candidate generation. Each call writes the raw memory
records to a temporary file, whose path replaces {context_path}. Then
the Executor Agent reads or searches that file using local tools and
returns a structured JSON report. The summary prompt consolidates useful
and weak patterns, unresolved questions, and recommendations. The
stagnation prompt identifies overused mechanisms and proposes a
structural change, with a concrete instruction for the next generation
step. Reports are stored in memory, with each newly generated report
replacing the previous active version of its type.

## Appendix F Seed and Evolved Harness Modules

This section presents the seed harnesses and representative
LLM-generated harnesses for SEMO and NSGA-II. These examples illustrate
how HEMO evolves adaptive search procedures that coordinate memory
retrieval, parent selection, and candidate generation using the search
feedback. The three modules of SEMO harness 141 and the four modules of
NSGA-II harness 98 originally span 416 and 1,241 source lines,
respectively. For readability, we present their core mechanisms with
concise module descriptions and summarize omitted implementation details
in comments. Captions report validation HV and runtime in seconds.

\# seed retrieve_memory

"""Retrieve valid records matching the task, family, representation and
objective dimensions, prioritizing Pareto candidates. The template also
allows quality or runtime preferences and recent summary or stagnation
reports when useful; the seed uses a fixed Pareto query."""

def retrieve_memory(self, \*\*kwargs):

memory_top_k = 5

query = {’family’: self.task_descriptor.get(’family’,
self.task_descriptor.get(’problem_family’)),

’representation’: self.task_descriptor.get(’representation’), ’tasks’:
\[self.task_id\],

’objective_dims’: \[self.task_descriptor.get(’objective_dim’)\],
’valid’: True, ’on_pareto_pf’: True}

records = self.memory_fs.query(task_id=self.task_id, query=query,
top_k=memory_top_k); return records

\# seed select_parent_algorithm

"""Rank valid scored heuristics by nondomination and crowding, then
sample one or two leading parents. Parent count sets the generation
context without prescribing mutation or crossover."""

def select_parent_algorithm(self, max_returned_parents=5, \*\*kwargs):

crossover_prob = 0.6; parent_top_pool_min_size = 4

valid = \[h for h in self.population if h.valid and h.score is not
None\]

if not valid: return \[\]

ordered = update_archive_by_crowding_distance(population=valid,
max_size=len(valid), score_key=’score’)

top_pool = ordered\[:min(len(ordered), max(parent_top_pool_min_size,
max_returned_parents))\]

if len(top_pool) \>= 2 and random.random() \< crossover_prob:
num_parents = 2

else: num_parents = 1

num_parents = min(num_parents, max_returned_parents, len(top_pool));
return random.sample(top_pool, k=num_parents)

\# seed evolve_target_algorithm

"""For each candidate, retrieve memory, select parents, apply heartbeat
once, then generate, evaluate and record through fixed helpers. Finalize
after the loop."""

def evolve_target_algorithm(self, budget):

trace = \[\]

for step in range(int(budget)):

memory_records = self.retrieve_memory(); parents =
self.select_parent_algorithm()

operator_decision = self.\_apply_heartbeat(step=step,
memory_records=memory_records)

candidate = self.\_generate_evaluate_record_candidate(...)

return self.\_finalize_harness_output(trace)

retrieve_memory retrieves valid Pareto records for the current task.
select_parent_algorithm samples one or two parents from candidates

evolve_target_algorithm repeats retrieval, parent selection, generation,

\# seed retrieve_memory

"""Query up to ten valid records matching task, family and
representation, covering operators, combinations and interactions;
return a list."""

def retrieve_memory(self, \*\*kwargs):

memory_top_k = 10

query = {’family’: self.task_descriptor.get(’family’,
self.task_descriptor.get(’problem_family’)),

’representation’: self.task_descriptor.get(’representation’), ’tasks’:
\[self.task_id\], ’valid’: True,

’text’: \[’operator’, ’combination’, ’interaction’\]}

records = self.memory_fs.query(task_id=self.task_id, query=query,
top_k=memory_top_k); return list(records or \[\])

\# seed select_target_algorithm

"""Rotate deterministically through operator slots in their declared
order, starting at the first slot. Return the chosen target with a
reason."""

def select_target_algorithm(self, memory_records, \*\*kwargs):

if self.last_selected_operator not in self.operator_names: selected_idx
= 0

else:

previous_idx = self.operator_names.index(self.last_selected_operator)

selected_idx = (previous_idx + 1) % len(self.operator_names)

target_operator = self.operator_names\[selected_idx\]

return TargetOperatorDecision(target_operator=target_operator,

reason=’Deterministic coordinate rotation over all executable
solver-operator slots.’)

\# seed select_parent_algorithm

"""Keep valid candidates for the target slot, favoring archive
improvements. Include the current implementation as fallback and return
at most six."""

def select_parent_algorithm(self, target_operator, memory_records,
\*\*kwargs):

max_returned_parents = 6

population = \[candidate for candidate in
self.operator_populations.get(target_operator,

\[\]) if candidate.valid and candidate.code and (candidate.operator_name
== target_operator)\]

current_operator =
self.current_combination.operators.get(target_operator)

if current_operator is not None and all((candidate.id !=
current_operator.id for candidate in population)):

population.append(current_operator)

if not population: return \[\]

population.sort(key=lambda candidate: (not
bool(candidate.meta.get(’improved_combination_archive’, False)),

candidate.id))

return population\[:max_returned_parents\]

\# seed evolve_target_algorithm

"""Deduplicate valid nondominated parents by code and generate from each
unique unordered pair. Then sample nondominated parents for individual
offspring, using mutation_rate and remaining budget to limit their
number. Refresh the parent pool and repeat within the inner budget."""

def evolve_target_algorithm(self, target_operator, operator_parents,
memory_records, episode_context, inner_budget,

start_eval_step, trace, \*\*kwargs):

mutation_rate = 0.2; outer_step = int(kwargs.get(’outer_step’, 0));

b = mode_beta.get(m, {’alpha’: 1.0, ’beta’: 1.0}); a =
float(b.get(’alpha’, 1.0))

bb = float(b.get(’beta’, 1.0))

try:

ts_sample = random.betavariate(max(1e-06, a), max(1e-06, bb))

except Exception:

ts_sample = a / (a + bb) if a + bb \> 0 else 0.5

stats = mode_stats.get(m, {’reward_sum’: 0.0, ’count’: 0.0}); count =
float(stats.get(’count’, 0.0))

reward_sum = float(stats.get(’reward_sum’, 0.0)); mean_r = reward_sum /
count if count \> 0 else 0.0

bonus = c_ucb \* math.sqrt(max(0.0, math.log(float(total_plays) + 1.0))
/ (count + 1.0))

bias = exploit_bias_late \* max(0.0, min(1.0, progress)) if m ==
’exploit’ else 0.0

val = float(ts_weight) \* float(ts_sample) + float(mean_r) +
float(bonus) + float(bias)

if val \> best_val: best_val = val; mode = m

and weakest-objective focus for

candidate, update_out =
self.\_generate_evaluate_record_operator_candidate(...)

candidate_ids.append(getattr(candidate, ’id’, None))

... \# OMITTED: Compute score sum, improvement flag, and nonnegative
gain delta against best_sum.

if is_improved: reward = float(improved_base) + float(credit_gain) \*
float(delta)

elif bool(getattr(candidate, ’valid’, False)) and math.isfinite(ssum):
reward = float(small_valid_bonus)

else: reward = 0.0

mb = mode_beta.get(mode, {’alpha’: 1.0, ’beta’: 1.0})

if is_improved: mb\[’alpha’\] = float(mb.get(’alpha’, 1.0)) + 1.0

else: mb\[’beta’\] = float(mb.get(’beta’, 1.0)) + 1.0

mode_beta\[mode\] = mb

float(mode_stats\[mode\].get(’reward_sum’, 0.0)) + float(reward)

mode_stats\[mode\]\[’count’\] = float(mode_stats\[mode\].get(’count’,
0.0)) + 1.0

if bool(getattr(candidate, ’valid’, False)) and math.isfinite(ssum):

if ssum \< best_sum: best_sum = ssum; best_cand = candidate; best_vec =
score_vector(candidate)

for k in list(parent_credits.keys()): parent_credits\[k\] =
float(parent_credits\[k\]) \* float(contribution_decay)

inc = float(reward) / float(max(1, len(current_parents)))

for p in current_parents:

pid = getattr(p, ’id’, None)

if isinstance(pid, str): parent_credits\[pid\] = parent_credits.get(pid,
0.0) + float(inc)

maintain_pool(updated_pool)

fail_streak = 0 if is_improved else fail_streak + 1

return {’target_operator’: target_operator, ’num_evaluated’:
int(inner_budget), ’candidate_ids’: candidate_ids}

during self-evolution (ID 98). Bi-TSP validation
$`(\mathrm{HV},\mathrm{runtime})=(0.468633,1.656327\,\mathrm{s})`$.
retrieve_memory interleaves evidence about quality, runtime, operator
interactions, and related tasks, adding failures and reports when
indicated by search history. select_target_algorithm ranks operator
slots using gains, failures, and exploration signals, matching past
evidence to the other operators in the current combination.
select_parent_algorithm balances quality, diversity, novelty, and
compatibility with that combination. evolve_target_algorithm combines
Beta sampling, observed rewards, and a UCB bonus to select generation
modes, and updates parent credit from offspring outcomes. Compared with
the seed’s fixed rotation and pairing schedule, this design makes target
and parent choices sensitive to operator interactions and adapts
generation guidance to the observed outcomes.

## Appendix G Why Discounted Credit is Suitable for Stateful Harness Self-Evolution

HEMO assigns credit to the decision module updated at each outer step
according to the downstream multi-objective performance of the resulting
harness state. The improvement from parent to child is normalized and
clipped to $`[-1,1]`$ for each score dimension, and the module reward is
their average. Hence, $`r_{t}\in[-1,1]`$. The expected utility of a
module depends on the current harness state:

|     |                                                           |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu_{m,t}=\mathbb{E}\left[r_{t}\mid m_{t}=m,H_{t}\right].
       ```                                                        |     |

As other decision modules change, the expected benefit of updating
module $`m`$ may also change. Module selection in HEMO is therefore
naturally modeled as a nonstationary credit assignment problem.

### G-A Attenuation of Stale Module Credit

For each module $`m`$, HEMO maintains a discounted selection count and
reward sum,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}=\gamma n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t-1}+\mathbf{1}\{m_{t}=m\},\qquad R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}=\gamma R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t-1}+\mathbf{1}\{m_{t}=m\}r_{t},
``` |  |

where $`\gamma\in(0,1)`$. Equivalently, an observation collected at
outer step $`s`$ contributes with weight $`\gamma^{t-s}`$ at step $`t`$.

Proposition 1 (Geometric attenuation of stale credit). Consider an outer
step $`\tau`$ after which the harness enters a different search regime.
Let

|     |                                                                |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       W^{-}_{m,t}=\sum_{s\leq\tau}\mathbf{1}\{m_{s}=m\}\gamma^{t-s}.
       ```                                                             |     |

denote the total weight at step $`t>\tau`$ assigned to observations of
module $`m`$ collected no later than $`\tau`$. Then

|     |                                            |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       W^{-}_{m,t}=\gamma^{t-\tau}W^{-}_{m,\tau}.
       ```                                         |     | (35) |

Proof. Factoring $`\gamma^{t-\tau}`$ from the definition gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
W^{-}_{m,t}=\gamma^{t-\tau}\sum_{s\leq\tau}\mathbf{1}\{m_{s}=m\}\gamma^{\tau-s}=\gamma^{t-\tau}W^{-}_{m,\tau}.
``` |  |

Since $`\gamma\in(0,1)`$, credit collected under earlier harness states
loses weight geometrically as the outer trajectory proceeds. $`\square`$

This attenuation does not require module $`m`$ to be selected again. By
comparison, an undiscounted estimator retains unit weight for every
historical observation until additional observations of the same module
dilute their influence.

To illustrate the effect on module utility, consider a local model in
which the mean reward is $`\mu_{m}^{-}`$ up to $`\tau`$ and
$`\mu_{m}^{+}`$ afterward. Let $`W^{+}_{m,t}`$ denote the discounted
weight of observations collected after $`\tau`$. For
$`W^{-}_{m,t}+W^{+}_{m,t}>0`$, define the weighted average of these
means as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mu}_{m,t}=\frac{W^{-}_{m,t}\mu_{m}^{-}+W^{+}_{m,t}\mu_{m}^{+}}{W^{-}_{m,t}+W^{+}_{m,t}}.
``` |  |

Then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left|\widetilde{\mu}_{m,t}-\mu_{m}^{+}\right|=\frac{W^{-}_{m,t}}{W^{-}_{m,t}+W^{+}_{m,t}}\left|\mu_{m}^{-}-\mu_{m}^{+}\right|.
``` |  |

Together with
Eq. ([35](#A7.E35 "In G-A Attenuation of Stale Module Credit ‣ Appendix G Why Discounted Credit is Suitable for Stateful Harness Self-Evolution ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")),
this identity shows that, as new observations of module $`m`$ accumulate
after the change, the relative contribution of earlier observations to
this weighted average decreases.

### G-B Recovery of Exploration Pressure

Discounting also affects modules that have not been selected recently.
Let

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N_{t}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}}n^{(\gamma)}_{j,t},\qquad b_{m,t}=c\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+N_{t})}{n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}}}
``` |  |

denote the total discounted count and the UCB exploration bonus,
respectively.

Proposition 2 (Exploration recovery for an unselected module). Suppose
module $`m`$ has previously been selected but is not selected during the
following $`\ell`$ outer steps. Then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t+\ell}=\gamma^{\ell}n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t},\qquad\bar{r}^{(\gamma)}_{m,t+\ell}=\bar{r}^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}.
``` |  |

Moreover, because exactly one module is selected at every outer step,
$`N_{t+\ell}\geq 1`$, giving

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{m,t+\ell}\geq c\sqrt{\frac{\log 2}{\gamma^{\ell}n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}}}.
``` |  | (36) |

Proof. When $`m`$ is not selected, its discounted count and reward sum
are both multiplied by $`\gamma`$ at every outer step. After $`\ell`$
steps,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t+\ell}=\gamma^{\ell}n^{(\gamma)}_{m,t},\qquad R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t+\ell}=\gamma^{\ell}R^{(\gamma)}_{m,t}.
``` |  |

Their ratio is unchanged, while substituting the discounted count and
$`N_{t+\ell}\geq 1`$ into the exploration bonus gives
Eq. ([36](#A7.E36 "In G-B Recovery of Exploration Pressure ‣ Appendix G Why Discounted Credit is Suitable for Stateful Harness Self-Evolution ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")).
For $`0<\gamma<1`$, this lower bound for the bonus at time $`t+\ell`$
increases with $`\ell`$ at a rate proportional to $`\gamma^{-\ell/2}`$.
Thus, the longer module $`m`$ remains unselected, the larger its
guaranteed exploration bonus becomes, increasing its opportunity to be
selected again even without an improvement in its estimated reward.
$`\square`$

Key Takeaway. Discounting provides two properties that are useful for
stateful harness self-evolution. Credit collected under earlier harness
states is attenuated geometrically, and modules that have not been
selected recently receive larger exploration bonuses as their discounted
counts decrease, making them more likely to be selected again. Together,
these effects allow the scheduler to respond when the utility of a
module changes after other parts of the harness have been updated.

These results do not imply that discounted UCB universally dominates
standard UCB. In a stationary setting, retaining the complete history
can provide a more accurate estimate of a fixed module utility. In HEMO,
however, module utility depends on the evolving harness state, so
discounting exchanges some statistical efficiency under stationarity for
greater responsiveness to changing module utility. This motivation is
consistent with established analyses of discounted UCB for nonstationary
bandit problems \[[57](#bib.bib63)\].

## Appendix H Experimental Details

### H-A Memory Filesystem and Record Schema

HEMO maintains a filesystem-based memory that persists optimization
experience across successive harness states. Fixed evaluation API and
memory logging routines ensure that different harness states produce
records under a common schema. Evaluated candidates are stored as
structured candidate records following the MemoryRecord schema, while
diagnostic summaries and stagnation reports are maintained as distinct
report records within the same memory filesystem.

Table [XIII](#A8.T13 "TABLE XIII ‣ H-A Memory Filesystem and Record Schema ‣ Appendix H Experimental Details ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
summarizes the fields most relevant to experience retrieval and the
memory context exposed to subsequent AOD steps. The schema combines task
information, evaluation outcomes, search lineage, and multi-objective
status. In particular, improved_archive, on_pareto_pf, high_hv, and
low_runtime provide compact descriptors of a candidate’s contribution
and current position in the candidate archive. The Pareto related
annotations are updated as the active archive changes, while the
original score vector remains available for detailed comparison. These
Pareto annotations expose whether a candidate contributes to the current
nondominated archive and which region of the quality–efficiency
trade-off it represents. Such information is useful because
multi-objective archives are designed not only to retain high-quality
solutions, but also to preserve convergence and diversity across
competing objectives \[[64](#bib.bib31), [65](#bib.bib22)\]. In HEMO,
these archive statistics are retained as explicit memory attributes so
that later search decisions can access this information directly.

For backbones with multiple interacting operators, the memory
additionally records the target operator through target_operator and the
operator composition mainly through operator_constitution and
combination_context. This preserves the context in which an operator
produced its observed performance, allowing subsequent search decisions
to reason about interactions among algorithmic components instead of
treating each operator candidate in isolation. Such context is important
because alternative designs of the same operator can exhibit different
strengths and inheritance relationships, while operators with different
functional roles may interact through complementary, conflicting, or
mutually exclusive effects \[[19](#bib.bib36)\]. Prior work on
multi-operator evolutionary search similarly shows that combining
operators with complementary behaviors and coordinating their usage can
be critical to overall search performance \[[66](#bib.bib20),
[67](#bib.bib21)\].

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Role |  Memory field |  Meaning and type |
|  Retrieval scope |  task_id |  Task associated with the record (str), used to restrict retrieval to the current task or related scope. |
|  |  family, representation |  Problem family and solution representation (Optional\[str\]), used for matching related search experience. |
|  |  objective_dims |  Objective dimensionalities represented by the record (List\[str\], List\[int\]). |
|  |  timestamp |  Record creation time (float), providing a weak recency preference during retrieval. |
|      Evaluation  context |  score |  Observed candidate score vector (Any, normally a numeric list), typically containing negative HV and per-instance runtime. |
|  |  valid, error |  Evaluation validity and failure information (Optional\[bool\], Optional\[str\]). |
|  |  improved_archive |  Whether the candidate improved the candidate archive when first evaluated (Optional\[bool\]). |
|  |  on_pareto_pf |  Whether the candidate or operator combination currently belongs to the active Pareto archive (bool). |
|  |  high_hv, low_runtime |  Indicators of relatively strong HV or runtime among active Pareto records (bool). Whether the record is above the median in HV or below the median in runtime among active candidate Pareto records, respectively. |
|  |  |  |
|  Search context |  parent_ids, used_memory_ids |  Parent candidates and historical records used during generation (List\[str\]). |
|  |  description, summary |  Textual description of the candidate and a compact summary of its search outcome (str). |
|      Operator  interaction |  target_operator |  Operator selected for modification in a multi-operator solver (Optional\[str\]). |
|  |  context_operator_ids |  Identifiers of the accompanying operators in the evaluated composition (Dict\[str, str\]). |
|  |  operator_constitution |  Complete operator composition associated with the observed evaluation result (Dict\[str, Any\]). |
|  |  combination_context |  Textual description of the operator combination and its search context (str). |

TABLE XIII: Memory fields most relevant to experience retrieval and
subsequent search decisions.

Under the SEMO backbone, the instance settings and evaluation protocol
for TSP, Bi-CVRP, and Bi-KP follow MPaGE \[[18](#bib.bib34)\]. Under
NSGA-II, the benchmark construction and design protocol for FJSP follow

pipeline with the problem-specific configurations described in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmark Problems ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization").

|  TSP |  Bi-TSP |  20 cities |  10 |  20 cities |  10 |
|  |  Tri-TSP |  20 cities |  10 |  20 cities |  10 |

TABLE XIV: Problem sizes and numbers of instances used for heuristic or
operator design.

HEMO self-evolution and inference settings. For both backbones, the
initial harness population contains five harness states. The discounted
UCB scheduler uses discount factor $`\gamma=0.98`$ and exploration
coefficient $`c=\sqrt{2}`$. During inference, the candidate population
size is 20 for SEMO, and, for NSGA-II, the population size of each
operator type and the complete operator combination population size are
both set to 20. For same-task inference, up to the latest 1,000 memory
records collected during harness self-evolution are loaded to warm-start
the memory filesystem. In intra-family cross-task inference, no
source-task memory is transferred and the target task starts with a
fresh memory filesystem. The LLM temperature is set to 1.0 for all
models used.

For inference, we exclude harness states produced during initialization
and select one state from the remaining harness state Pareto archive
using normalized Euclidean distance to the empirical ideal point. Let
$`\mathcal{H}`$ denote the eligible harness states and let
$`\mathbf{s}(H)=(s_{1}(H),\ldots,s_{D}(H))`$ denote the lower-is-better
harness score vector. For each dimension,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{d}^{\mathrm{ideal}}=\min_{H\in\mathcal{H}}s_{d}(H),\qquad z_{d}^{\mathrm{nadir}}=\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}s_{d}(H).
``` |  |

We normalize each harness score as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{s}_{d}(H)=\frac{s_{d}(H)-z_{d}^{\mathrm{ideal}}}{z_{d}^{\mathrm{nadir}}-z_{d}^{\mathrm{ideal}}},
``` |  |

with $`\tilde{s}_{d}(H)=0`$ when the denominator is zero, and select

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H^{*}=\arg\min_{H\in\mathcal{H}}\sqrt{\sum_{d=1}^{D}\tilde{s}_{d}(H)^{2}}.
``` |  |

Thus, the ideal point is empirical, formed from the best observed value
of each harness score dimension among the eligible harness states. The
selected harness is subsequently fixed during inference on both the
source task and the related task used for intra-family transfer.

Traditional MOEA baselines. We implement SEMO,
NSGA-II \[[7](#bib.bib15)\], MOEA/D \[[8](#bib.bib16)\], and
PFG-MOEA \[[37](#bib.bib65)\] within our evaluation pipeline, using
task-specific representations and variation operators. SEMO uses the
fixed seed heuristic operator provided for operator design, while
NSGA-II uses the corresponding seed operator combination without
modification by an LLM. MOEA/D reuses task-specific seed operators,
applying segment relocation, reversal, and multi-segment modification to
Bi-TSP and Tri-TSP, relocation, swap, and segment reversal to Bi-CVRP
and Bi-SPDP, and bit-flip mutation, uniform crossover, and repair-based
mutation to Bi-KP and Bi-MDKP. For PFG-MOEA, we use partially mapped
crossover and swap mutation on Bi-TSP, Tri-TSP, and Bi-CVRP, and uniform
crossover followed by bit-flip mutation and feasibility repair on Bi-KP
and Bi-MDKP. These operator types follow the permutation and binary
variation choices described by MPaGE \[[18](#bib.bib34)\]. For Bi-SPDP,
PFG-MOEA instead reuses the task-specific relocation, swap, and reversal
operators with signed-permutation repair. The task-specific decoders and
feasibility safeguards are retained in all implementations. For Bi-FJSP
and Tri-FJSP, NSGA-II, MOEA/D, and PFG-MOEA use the seed
operation-priority crossover and mutation, followed by
machine-assignment crossover and mutation.

LLM-based AOD baselines. We preserve the search mechanisms and
hyperparameters of the original LLM-based AOD frameworks, with two
common controls for comparison. The heuristic or operator population
size is set to 20 for EoH \[[14](#bib.bib11)\],
MEoH \[[17](#bib.bib32)\], MPaGE \[[18](#bib.bib34)\], and
E2OC \[[19](#bib.bib36)\], matching the population size used during HEMO
inference. Each method terminates when the same maximum number of
generated operator candidates is reached. All CPU-based evaluations were
conducted on AMD EPYC 9555 processors. Traditional MOEAs and LLM-based
AOD methods were configured to evaluate five instances of the same
problem size in parallel. For final testing, every solver configuration
is independently evaluated five times, and the mean performance over
these runs is used as its reported performance to reduce stochastic
variation from the underlying MOEA.

HEMO self-evolution cost breakdown. Harness self-evolution introduces a
one-time computational cost from evaluating candidate harness states.
For Bi-KP with the SEMO backbone, self-evolution on the source task
requires approximately 37.67 wall-clock hours and \$4.22 in GPT-4.1-nano
API calling cost on average. For Bi-CVRP with NSGA-II, the corresponding
process requires approximately 80.08 hours and \$12.67 in API calling
cost on average. Across all four source-task settings and independent
runs, the largest wall-clock runtime is about 216.56 hours and the
largest GPT-4.1-nano token cost is about \$29.52. The Claude Opus 4.8
Proposer and GPT-5 Realizer incur average costs of approximately \$12.53
and \$21.80 per complete run, respectively, across all source tasks.
This self-evolution cost is a one-time investment for obtaining the
evolved harness and accumulated optimization memory. The resulting
harness is subsequently reused during inference and intra-family
transfer without repeating harness self-evolution, reducing the need to
rediscover favorable quality–runtime trade-off regions from scratch.

## Appendix I Additional Experiments

### I-A Comparison with Expert-Designed TSP Operators

To further assess the quality of the operator combinations produced by
HEMO, we compare the best-HV operator combinations of NSGA-II designed
by HEMO (HEMO-NSGA-II) with several commonly used expert-designed TSP
operators and their sequential compositions. We do not include OX-based
combinations, as OX is outside the three operator interfaces considered
in our NSGA-II TSP backbone. Moreover, the expert comparison in
E2OC \[[19](#bib.bib36)\] shows that augmenting OX and swap with
additional local-search operators generally degrades performance
relative to the corresponding expert configurations. We therefore
evaluate the three operators individually, three sequential
compositions, E2OC, and the operator combination generated by HEMO on
Bi-TSP with $`N\in\{20,50,100\}`$.

TABLE XVI: Additional FJSP results with the SEMO backbone. ID comprises

including ties, and “–” denotes runs exceeding the time limit.

Table [XV](#A9.T15 "TABLE XV ‣ I-A Comparison with Expert-Designed TSP Operators ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
shows that HEMO achieves the highest HV at $`N=50`$ and $`N=100`$, while
2-opt remains slightly better at $`N=20`$. Averaged across the three
problem sizes, HEMO obtains the highest HV, clearly exceeding the
strongest expert operator, 2-opt, and outperforming E2OC. This result is
notable because several manually composed operator sequences perform
substantially worse than the strongest individual operators, indicating
that simply combining multiple neighborhood operators does not guarantee
better search performance.

The operator combination designed by HEMO also achieves a favorable
runtime profile. It achieves a $`1.911\times`$ speedup relative to the
slowest method, while attaining a runtime close to that of the fastest
operator combination at the largest problem size. Some expert
combinations execute faster, but exhibit considerably lower HV. These
results provide additional evidence that HEMO can discover operator
combinations that remain competitive with strong expert operators in
both solution quality and computational efficiency.

### I-B Additional Results with the SEMO Backbone

Table [XVI](#A9.T16 "TABLE XVI ‣ I-A Comparison with Expert-Designed TSP Operators ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
reports additional results on Bi-FJSP and Tri-FJSP. HEMO achieves the
highest OOD HV on both tasks. On Bi-FJSP, MPaGE achieves a slightly
higher overall HV, while HEMO has the lowest runtime among the LLM-based
AOD methods across all reported splits. On Tri-FJSP, HEMO achieves the
highest overall HV and the lowest overall runtime among the LLM-based
AOD methods, although MEoH is faster on the OOD instances. These results
highlight the effectiveness of the learned heuristics on the OOD
instances, despite not achieving the highest HV on the design
distribution used during harness self-evolution.

### I-C Additional Results with the NSGA-II Backbone

Table [XVII](#A9.T17 "TABLE XVII ‣ I-C Additional Results with the NSGA-II Backbone ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
reports results with the NSGA-II backbone on the multi-objective routing
tasks and the knapsack tasks. Expert, E2OC, and HEMO are compared within
the same NSGA-II backbone using HV, IGD, and runtime. For the NSGA-II
experiments on Bi-KP and Bi-MDKP, each objective is the negative
selected profit divided by the total available profit for that
objective:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{k}(\mathbf{x})=-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(k)}x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(k)}},\qquad k\in\{1,2\}.
``` |  | (37) |

HV is computed in this normalized minimization space with reference
point $`\mathbf{r}=(0,0)`$. The bounding ideal point is
$`\mathbf{z}=(-1,-1)`$. This protocol is shared by all three methods and
differs from the protocol used in the SEMO knapsack experiments. Their
HV values are therefore not directly comparable across backbones, and
the test instances also follow different generation procedures.

HEMO achieves the highest HV in nine of the twelve settings and the
lowest IGD in nine settings. On Bi-CVRP, it achieves the highest HV at
every size and the lowest IGD at sizes 50 and 100. On Bi-SPDP, HEMO
still achieves the lowest IGD at all three sizes and the highest HV at
sizes 50 and 100, though E2OC has a slightly higher HV at size 20. On
Bi-KP, HEMO achieves the highest HV at all sizes, while E2OC achieves
the lowest IGD at size 50 and HEMO achieves the lowest IGD at sizes 100
and 200. On Bi-MDKP, E2OC has the highest HV at sizes 50 and 100 and the
lowest IGD at size 50. HEMO achieves the lowest IGD at sizes 100 and
200, the highest HV at size 200, and the lowest runtime at all three
sizes. Overall, both quality indicators generally favor HEMO,
highlighting its effectiveness and generalization ability across both
routing and knapsack tasks.

### I-D Visualization of Obtained Solutions

Figures [4](#A9.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ I-D Visualization of Obtained Solutions ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
and [5](#A9.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ I-D Visualization of Obtained Solutions ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
compare the final solution fronts obtained using operators evolved by
HEMO with those produced by traditional MOEAs on Bi-KP, Bi-MDKP, Bi-TSP,
and Tri-TSP at three problem sizes. These comparisons complement the
aggregate HV and IGD results by illustrating the objective trade-offs
achieved by the designed operators on both source and transfer tasks.

With the SEMO backbone,
Figure [4](#A9.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ I-D Visualization of Obtained Solutions ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
compares HEMO with SEMO, NSGA-II, MOEA/D, and PFG-MOEA. The advantage is
particularly visible on the TSP tasks: HEMO reaches regions with shorter
distances across objectives, with a clear separation from several
baselines at larger problem sizes. The knapsack solution distributions
overlap more strongly, showing that the advantage depends on the
specific tasks.

With the NSGA-II backbone,
Figure [5](#A9.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ I-D Visualization of Obtained Solutions ‣ Appendix I Additional Experiments ‣ HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization")
compares HEMO-designed operators with the expert-designed operator
combination. The improved solution distributions on Bi-TSP and Tri-TSP
show that the learned operators remain effective when transferred from
two to three objectives. On Bi-KP and Bi-MDKP, the distributions overlap
more, while the quantitative results show higher HV for HEMO at every
displayed size. Together, these results illustrate the ability of
HEMO-designed heuristics to discover competitive trade-offs beyond those
obtained with fixed expert-designed heuristics.

## Appendix J Representative Discovered Heuristics and Operator Combinations

In this section, we give representative examples of two LLM-evolved
operator designs, with Bi-TSP under SEMO and Bi-KP under NSGA-II
providing comparisons with MPaGE and E2OC, respectively. For HEMO, each
box pairs a concise natural-language explanation with the complete
executable heuristic or operator implementation. Code formatting and
comments are condensed without changing the algorithmic logic. For each
candidate, we provide its design idea, reported score, unique
identifier, and an excerpt of the algorithm code. These examples
characterize particular discovered designs, while aggregate performance
is evaluated in the broader experimental results.

### J-A Bi-TSP with SEMO: HEMO and MPaGE

Both selected heuristics first filter the solution archive by Pareto
dominance and use randomly weighted, normalized tour costs to select a
parent tour. They differ mainly in neighborhood construction, with MPaGE
sampling from a broader menu, whereas HEMO pairs block relocation with
segment reversal and explicitly removes duplicate neighbors. Neither
implementation requires improvement over the parent, as each returns the
best sampled neighbor with a swap fallback if it coincides with the
parent. Thus, the comparison concerns how a bounded neighborhood is
explored.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Compared with MPaGE, HEMO uses a similar sampling budget to explore two
complementary changes to each sampled segment, moving it elsewhere in
the tour or reversing its order. This gives each segment two ways to
improve the tour, while deduplication avoids evaluating the same
neighbor repeatedly. Together with removing the explicit no-operation
option, this focuses computation on distinct alternatives. Symmetric
scalarization weights also give both objectives equal emphasis across
search steps. These mechanisms make more effective use of the sampling
budget, consistent with the selected heuristic’s higher HV and lower
runtime.

### J-B Bi-KP with NSGA-II: HEMO and E2OC

The selected combinations contain three binary-chromosome operators:
kp_bitflip, kp_crossover, and kp_repair_mutation. Both designs use
profit and weight information. The principal distinction is where
randomized profit scalarization enters the combination and whether
repair preserves the incoming chromosome. E2OC constructs new greedy
solutions in its repair operator, whereas HEMO combines scalarized
construction with mutation and uses its final repair operator to modify
the incoming solution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

E2OC’s final repair rebuilds from an empty selection, discarding the
mutation and crossover results. In HEMO, mutation mixes the incoming
solution with a greedy selection under a random objective preference,
while repair preserves and refines the result. Wider objective weights
encourage exploration near either objective extreme, and complementary
crossover preserves both parents’ bit values across the two children
before repair. Final repair fills unused capacity and allows feasible
exchanges favoring higher-density items. Together, these choices explore
diverse trade-offs while retaining useful inherited combinations.
````
